title: 1.1 agentic-loops / lifecycle
stem: A developer's customer support agent sometimes terminates prematurely because they check if response.content[0].type == 'text' to determine completion. The agent stops even when Claude has more tools to call. What is the bug and how should they fix it?

options.A: Add an iteration cap of 15 loops to ensure the agent runs long enough
options.B: Check the stop_reason field instead of content type — continue when stop_reason is 'tool_use', terminate when 'end_turn'
options.C: Parse the assistant's text for phrases like 'I have completed' before terminating
options.D: Set tool_choice to 'any' so Claude always calls a tool instead of returning text

why_correct: The stop_reason field is the deterministic, authoritative signal for loop control. Claude can return text alongside tool_use blocks, so checking content type is unreliable.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Arbitrary caps do not address the root cause. The agent exits because it misidentifies the response type, not because it loops insufficient times.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Natural language parsing is ambiguous and unreliable. The stop_reason field already provides an unambiguous signal.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: This forces tool use even when the agent is genuinely finished, creating an infinite loop rather than fixing the detection logic.

exam_takeaway: The stop_reason field is the deterministic, authoritative signal for loop control. Claude can return text alongside tool_use blocks, so checking content type is unreliable.

title: 1.2 orchestration-patterns / decomposition
stem: A multi-agent research system produces a report on 'renewable energy technologies' that only covers solar and wind, missing geothermal, tidal, biomass, and nuclear fusion. Each subagent produced thorough coverage of its assigned topic. Where is the root cause?

options.A: The web search subagent's search queries were too narrow
options.B: The synthesis subagent failed to identify gaps in the research
options.C: The coordinator's task decomposition only assigned solar and wind as subtopics, missing other renewable energy categories
options.D: The document analysis subagent did not have access to sources covering other energy types

why_correct: The coordinator is responsible for decomposing the broad topic into subtopics. If it only assigns solar and wind, no downstream agent can cover the missing categories. Trace failures to their origin.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: The web search subagent researched what it was assigned. The issue is what it was assigned, not how it searched.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: The synthesis agent can only work with the research it receives. It cannot synthesise topics that were never researched.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Source availability is not the issue. The coordinator never asked any agent to research geothermal, tidal, biomass, or fusion.

exam_takeaway: The coordinator is responsible for decomposing the broad topic into subtopics. If it only assigns solar and wind, no downstream agent can cover the missing categories. Trace failures to their origin.

title: 1.3 guardrails-safety / structured-metadata
stem: A synthesis agent produces a report with several claims that have no source attribution. The web search and document analysis subagents are working correctly and returning well-sourced results. What is the most likely root cause?

options.A: The synthesis agent's system prompt does not require citations
options.B: The coordinator is passing content to the synthesis agent without structured metadata (source URLs, document names, page numbers)
options.C: The web search subagent needs to return results in a different format
options.D: The synthesis agent needs access to the web search tool directly

why_correct: Context passing must include structured data that separates content from metadata. Without source URLs and document names, the synthesis agent has no attribution information to include.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Even with citation requirements in the prompt, the synthesis agent cannot attribute claims to sources if the metadata was never passed to it.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: The web search subagent is working correctly. The issue is how the coordinator passes its results to the synthesis agent.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Giving the synthesis agent web search tools violates the principle of scoped tool access and does not address the context passing failure.

exam_takeaway: Context passing must include structured data that separates content from metadata. Without source URLs and document names, the synthesis agent has no attribution information to include.

title: 1.4 claude-agent-sdk / prerequisite-gates
stem: Production data shows that in 8% of cases, a customer support agent processes refunds without verifying account ownership, occasionally leading to refunds on wrong accounts. What is the most appropriate fix?

options.A: Implement a programmatic prerequisite gate that blocks process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID
options.B: Add stronger instructions to the system prompt emphasising the importance of verification before refunds
options.C: Add few-shot examples showing the correct verification-then-refund workflow
options.D: Implement a routing classifier that sends refund requests to a specialised verification pipeline

why_correct: Financial operations require deterministic enforcement. A prerequisite gate physically prevents the refund tool from executing until identity verification is complete, eliminating the 8% failure rate entirely.

per_option_counter_explanations.B: The current system prompt already instructs verification but fails 8% of the time. Enhanced prompts reduce but do not eliminate the failure rate. Financial operations require deterministic guarantees.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Few-shot examples improve consistency but still have a non-zero failure rate. For financial operations, probabilistic improvements are insufficient.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: A routing classifier handles request routing, not per-agent workflow enforcement. The issue is within the agent's execution sequence, not how requests reach it.

exam_takeaway: Financial operations require deterministic enforcement. A prerequisite gate physically prevents the refund tool from executing until identity verification is complete, eliminating the 8% failure rate entirely.

title: 1.5 multi-agent-systems / pretooluse-enforcement
stem: An agent occasionally processes international transfers without required compliance checks. The compliance team requires 100% enforcement of anti-money laundering (AML) checks before any international transfer. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Add detailed AML check instructions to the system prompt with examples of correct behaviour
options.B: Implement a PreToolUse hook that blocks transfer execution until AML verification returns a pass result
options.C: Add a PostToolUse hook to flag completed transfers that skipped AML checks
options.D: Train the agent with few-shot examples showing the correct AML verification workflow

why_correct: A hook intercepts the outgoing tool call before execution and physically blocks it until the compliance check passes. This provides the deterministic guarantee that AML rules require.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Prompt instructions provide probabilistic compliance. With international transfers and AML regulations, a single failure could result in legal penalties. 100% enforcement requires deterministic guarantees.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: PostToolUse hooks run after execution. By the time the hook fires, the non-compliant transfer has already been processed. Prevention is required, not detection.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Few-shot examples improve accuracy but do not guarantee 100% compliance. Regulatory requirements demand deterministic enforcement via hooks.

exam_takeaway: A hook intercepts the outgoing tool call before execution and physically blocks it until the compliance check passes. This provides the deterministic guarantee that AML rules require.

title: 1.6 human-in-the-loop / attention-dilution
stem: A code review agent processes 14 files and produces detailed feedback for the first 5 files but misses obvious bugs in files 10-14. It also flags a pattern as problematic in one file while approving identical code in another. What is the root cause and solution?

options.A: The model's context window is too small — upgrade to a model with a larger context window
options.B: Split the review into per-file local analysis passes plus a separate cross-file integration pass
options.C: Add a stronger system prompt emphasising the importance of reviewing all files equally
options.D: Reduce the number of files reviewed per run to 5 and process in batches

why_correct: Multi-pass architecture solves attention dilution. Per-file passes ensure consistent depth for each file. The cross-file integration pass catches data flow issues and ensures consistent pattern evaluation.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Context window size is not the issue. Attention dilution occurs because processing too many items in a single pass produces inconsistent depth, regardless of window size.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Prompt improvements do not solve attention dilution. The fundamental issue is processing too many items in a single pass, which is an architectural problem requiring a structural solution.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Batching is closer to the right idea but misses the cross-file integration pass. Without it, cross-file data flow issues and pattern consistency are not addressed.

exam_takeaway: Multi-pass architecture solves attention dilution. Per-file passes ensure consistent depth for each file. The cross-file integration pass catches data flow issues and ensures consistent pattern evaluation.

title: 1.7 error-recovery-resilience / fresh-start
stem: A developer resumes a Claude Code session after modifying 3 files in a 50-file codebase. The agent gives contradictory advice about the modified files because it is reasoning from stale tool results. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Start a completely new session and re-analyse the entire codebase from scratch
options.B: Resume the session and ask the agent to re-read only the 3 modified files
options.C: Start a fresh session with an injected summary of prior findings and inform the agent about the specific 3 file changes for targeted re-analysis
options.D: Use fork_session to create a branch that incorporates the file changes

why_correct: A fresh session with summary injection avoids stale tool results. Specifying the 3 changed files enables targeted re-analysis without wasting time on unchanged files.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Re-analysing the entire 50-file codebase is wasteful when only 3 files changed. Targeted re-analysis is more efficient.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: Resuming preserves the stale tool results in context. The agent may still reason from outdated information for other decisions. A fresh start with summary injection is more reliable.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: fork_session creates an independent exploration branch from a shared baseline. It is for divergent approaches, not for updating stale context after file changes.

exam_takeaway: A fresh session with summary injection avoids stale tool results. Specifying the 3 changed files enables targeted re-analysis without wasting time on unchanged files.

title: 1.1 agentic-loops / anti-patterns
stem: A customer support agent runs to its `max_iterations=10` cap on every request, even simple ones. Logs show stop_reason returns 'end_turn' after the third iteration, but the loop ignores it and uses the iteration count as its primary termination signal. What architectural change resolves this?

options.A: Increase the iteration cap to 20 so the agent has more room to work on complex requests
options.B: Lower the iteration cap (for example to 3) so the loop is forced to terminate earlier on simple requests
options.C: Use stop_reason as the primary loop control — exit on 'end_turn', continue on 'tool_use' — and retain the iteration cap only as a safety backstop, not the primary termination mechanism
options.D: Parse the agent's response text after each iteration to detect phrases like 'task complete' and terminate early when found

why_correct: The stop_reason field is the authoritative signal for loop control. The loop should exit on 'end_turn' and continue on 'tool_use'. An iteration cap can remain as a safety net for edge cases, but must not be the primary stopping mechanism, which is the anti-pattern causing unnecessary iterations here.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Increasing the cap does not address the root cause. The agent already finishes simple tasks by iteration 3 (stop_reason is 'end_turn') but the loop ignores this signal and keeps running. A higher cap would waste even more iterations.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: This keeps the iteration count as the primary termination signal, which is the anti-pattern itself. Hard-coding a lower cap happens to fit this simple case but truncates genuinely complex requests that legitimately need more iterations, and it still ignores the stop_reason field that already reports completion. The fix is to make stop_reason the control signal, not to retune the cap.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Parsing natural language for completion signals is an anti-pattern. The model may use such phrases while still having tool calls queued, and may complete work without such phrases. The stop_reason field already provides a deterministic, unambiguous signal.

exam_takeaway: The stop_reason field is the authoritative signal for loop control. The loop should exit on 'end_turn' and continue on 'tool_use'. An iteration cap can remain as a safety net for edge cases, but must not be the primary stopping mechanism, which is the anti-pattern causing unnecessary iterations here.

title: 1.2 orchestration-patterns / coordinator
stem: A consulting firm's multi-agent research system has a coordinator that always invokes the full pipeline of five subagents (web search, document analysis, data extraction, synthesis, and formatting) for every query, including simple factual lookups that only need web search. This adds unnecessary latency and cost. What is the correct architectural fix?

options.A: Have the coordinator dynamically select which subagents to invoke based on query requirements, rather than always routing through the full pipeline
options.B: Allow subagents to communicate directly with each other so they can skip unnecessary steps in the pipeline
options.C: Add a caching layer so subagents that have no work to do return immediately
options.D: Split into two separate systems: one for simple queries and one for complex queries

why_correct: The coordinator should analyse query requirements and decide which subagents are needed. A simple factual lookup only needs the web search agent, not the full five-agent pipeline. Dynamic selection reduces latency and cost for straightforward requests.

per_option_counter_explanations.B: Direct subagent communication violates the hub-and-spoke architecture. All communication must flow through the coordinator. The fix is smarter coordinator routing, not bypassing the coordinator.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Caching does not address the architectural issue. Invoking subagents that are not needed adds API call overhead and latency regardless of whether results are cached. The coordinator should not invoke unnecessary subagents in the first place.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Maintaining two separate systems creates unnecessary complexity. The coordinator's role is precisely to analyse query requirements and make routing decisions. A single coordinator with dynamic selection handles both cases.

exam_takeaway: The coordinator should analyse query requirements and decide which subagents are needed. A simple factual lookup only needs the web search agent, not the full five-agent pipeline. Dynamic selection reduces latency and cost for straightforward requests.

sources.label: Lesson 1.2: Multi-Agent Orchestration (Coordinator responsibilities)

title: 1.3 guardrails-safety / parallel-spawning
stem: A multi-agent research system has a coordinator that spawns a web search subagent and a document analysis subagent sequentially across separate API turns. The web search completes in 8 seconds and the document analysis completes in 12 seconds, giving a total latency of 20 seconds. The two subagents are investigating independent topics and do not depend on each other's results. How should the architect reduce this latency?

options.A: Merge the web search and document analysis into a single subagent to reduce coordination overhead
options.B: Have the coordinator emit both Agent tool calls in a single response to spawn both subagents in parallel, reducing total latency to roughly 12 seconds
options.C: Allow the web search subagent to directly invoke the document analysis subagent after it finishes, removing the coordinator round-trip
options.D: Use fork_session to split the coordinator into two parallel branches, one for each subagent

why_correct: When subagents investigate independent topics, the coordinator can emit multiple Agent tool calls (renamed from Task tool in SDK v2.1.63) in a single response. Both subagents run concurrently, so total latency is determined by the slower one (12 seconds) rather than the sum (20 seconds).

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Merging agents violates the principle of specialised subagents with scoped tool access. It also does not reduce total processing time — the merged agent still needs to do both tasks, and loses the benefit of parallel execution.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Direct subagent communication violates the hub-and-spoke architecture where all communication flows through the coordinator. This also would not achieve parallel execution — it would still be sequential.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: fork_session is for divergent exploration of the same problem from a shared baseline, not for parallel subagent invocation. The Agent tool with parallel emission in a single coordinator response is the correct mechanism for spawning concurrent subagents.

exam_takeaway: When subagents investigate independent topics, the coordinator can emit multiple Agent tool calls (renamed from Task tool in SDK v2.1.63) in a single response. Both subagents run concurrently, so total latency is determined by the slower one (12 seconds) rather than the sum (20 seconds).

title: 1.4 claude-agent-sdk / handoff-protocols
stem: A customer support agent needs to escalate a complex billing dispute to a human agent. The AI agent compiles a handoff that includes the conversation summary and recommended action, but the human agent reports they cannot effectively resolve the issue because critical information is missing. Which missing element is most likely causing the problem?

options.A: The handoff is missing the AI agent's confidence score for its recommendation
options.B: The handoff is missing the full conversation transcript so the human agent can review exact customer messages
options.C: The handoff is missing the customer ID and root cause analysis, making it impossible for the human agent to look up the account or understand the underlying issue
options.D: The handoff should include links to internal knowledge base articles about the billing issue

why_correct: A structured handoff must include: customer ID, conversation summary, root cause analysis, refund amount (if applicable), and recommended action. Without the customer ID, the human agent cannot access the account. Without root cause analysis, they cannot understand the underlying problem. The human agent lacks the conversation transcript, so the handoff must be self-contained.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Confidence scores are not part of the required handoff protocol. The structured handoff requires customer ID, conversation summary, root cause analysis, refund amount if applicable, and recommended action.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: The handoff protocol explicitly accounts for the fact that human agents do NOT have access to the conversation transcript. The handoff summary must be self-contained, not reliant on a transcript.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Knowledge base links are not part of the structured handoff protocol. The human agent needs the customer ID, root cause analysis, and other required fields to effectively resolve the escalation.

exam_takeaway: A structured handoff must include: customer ID, conversation summary, root cause analysis, refund amount (if applicable), and recommended action. Without the customer ID, the human agent cannot access the account. Without root cause analysis, they cannot understand the underlying problem. The human agent lacks the conversation transcript, so the handoff must be self-contained.

sources.label: Lesson 1.4: Workflow Enforcement and Handoff (Structured handoff protocols)

title: 1.5 multi-agent-systems / posttooluse-normalisation
stem: A customer support agent integrates with three different backend systems via MCP tools. One system returns dates as Unix timestamps, another returns ISO 8601 strings, and the third returns dates in 'DD/MM/YYYY' format. The agent occasionally misinterprets dates, leading to incorrect order lookup results. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Add instructions to the system prompt explaining the three date formats and how to interpret each one
options.B: Standardise the backend APIs to all return the same date format
options.C: Implement a PreToolUse hook that converts all dates to ISO 8601 before passing them to the tools
options.D: Implement a PostToolUse hook that normalises all date formats to ISO 8601 before the model processes the results

why_correct: PostToolUse hooks intercept tool results after execution but before the model processes them. Converting all dates to a consistent ISO 8601 format ensures the model receives clean, unambiguous data regardless of which backend system produced it. This is the canonical use case for PostToolUse hooks.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Relying on the model to correctly interpret heterogeneous formats is unreliable. The model may confuse DD/MM/YYYY with MM/DD/YYYY or miscalculate Unix timestamps. Data normalisation should happen deterministically, not probabilistically.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: While ideal, modifying three separate backend systems is often impractical and outside the agent architect's control. The Agent SDK provides PostToolUse hooks precisely for normalising heterogeneous outputs without modifying upstream systems.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: PreToolUse hooks intercept outgoing calls before execution, not incoming results. Date normalisation needs to happen on tool results after execution. The correct hook type is PostToolUse, not PreToolUse.

exam_takeaway: PostToolUse hooks intercept tool results after execution but before the model processes them. Converting all dates to a consistent ISO 8601 format ensures the model receives clean, unambiguous data regardless of which backend system produced it. This is the canonical use case for PostToolUse hooks.

title: 1.6 human-in-the-loop / adaptive-decomposition
stem: A consulting firm needs an agent to add a comprehensive test suite to a large legacy codebase. The codebase has no existing tests, unclear dependencies between modules, and the team does not know which areas are most critical. Which task decomposition strategy is most appropriate?

options.A: A fixed sequential pipeline that reviews each file in alphabetical order and generates tests for each one
options.B: A single-pass analysis that processes the entire codebase at once and generates a complete test plan
options.C: Dynamic adaptive decomposition that starts by mapping the codebase structure, identifies high-impact areas, and creates a prioritised plan that adapts as dependencies emerge
options.D: A multi-pass architecture with per-file analysis and cross-file integration, identical to a code review pipeline

why_correct: Adding tests to a legacy codebase with unknown dependencies is an open-ended investigation task. Dynamic adaptive decomposition generates subtasks based on what is discovered at each step — first mapping the structure, then identifying critical areas, then adapting the test plan as dependency relationships emerge.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Fixed sequential pipelines are best for predictable, structured tasks. Adding tests to a legacy codebase with unclear dependencies is an open-ended investigation that requires adaptive exploration to discover which areas are most critical and how dependencies affect test design.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: A single-pass analysis of a large codebase would suffer from attention dilution, producing inconsistent coverage. Additionally, a single pass cannot adapt to discoveries about dependencies and critical areas that emerge during exploration.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Multi-pass architecture solves attention dilution for review tasks, but test generation in a legacy codebase requires adaptive exploration — understanding which modules are critical, discovering dependencies, and prioritising coverage. The decomposition must adapt to findings, not follow a fixed per-file pattern.

exam_takeaway: Adding tests to a legacy codebase with unknown dependencies is an open-ended investigation task. Dynamic adaptive decomposition generates subtasks based on what is discovered at each step — first mapping the structure, then identifying critical areas, then adapting the test plan as dependency relationships emerge.

title: 1.7 error-recovery-resilience / fork-session
stem: A research team is using Claude Code to analyse a large dataset. After completing an initial analysis, they want to explore two competing hypotheses: one using a statistical modelling approach and another using a machine learning approach. Both explorations should start from the same baseline analysis but proceed independently. Which session management strategy is correct?

options.A: Resume the session twice with --resume, once for each hypothesis, running them one after the other
options.B: Start two fresh sessions, each with an injected summary of the initial analysis, and explore one hypothesis in each
options.C: Use the initial session and explore both hypotheses sequentially, asking the agent to set aside the first approach before starting the second
options.D: Use fork_session to create two independent branches from the shared analysis baseline, exploring one hypothesis in each fork

why_correct: fork_session creates independent branches from a shared baseline, which is exactly the use case here. Both forks start from the complete initial analysis but proceed independently. Neither exploration contaminates the other, enabling a clean comparison of the two approaches.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Resuming the same session twice would mean the second resume inherits context from the first hypothesis exploration, contaminating the independent baseline. Each hypothesis needs to diverge from the original analysis, not from each other.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: While this avoids context contamination, it loses the full richness of the original analysis context. Fresh start with summary injection is best when tool results are stale. Here, the baseline analysis is still valid and both branches should start from the complete shared baseline.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Sequential exploration in the same session means the second hypothesis is influenced by the first — the agent carries context, conclusions, and biases from the first exploration. Independent exploration requires isolated branches.

exam_takeaway: fork_session creates independent branches from a shared baseline, which is exactly the use case here. Both forks start from the complete initial analysis but proceed independently. Neither exploration contaminates the other, enabling a clean comparison of the two approaches.

title: 1.3 guardrails-safety / agent-tool
stem: A coordinator agent should spawn specialist subagents for billing disputes and technical issues. Its system prompt describes the delegation workflow correctly, yet when it tries to invoke a subagent nothing happens: no subagent is created and no related error is thrown. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The coordinator's allowedTools list does not include 'Agent' (or its backward-compatible alias 'Task'), so it cannot invoke the mechanism for spawning subagents
options.B: The subagent's AgentDefinition is missing a description field, preventing it from being invoked
options.C: The coordinator needs to pass the full conversation history to the subagent for it to initialise properly
options.D: The subagents need to be pre-registered in a configuration file before the coordinator can invoke them

why_correct: The Agent tool (renamed from Task tool in SDK v2.1.63) is the mechanism for spawning subagents. If 'Agent' (or 'Task') is not in the coordinator's allowedTools, it physically cannot create subagents regardless of what the system prompt instructs. This is a configuration issue, not a prompt issue.

per_option_counter_explanations.B: A missing AgentDefinition description would cause issues with the subagent's behaviour, but the problem here is that the coordinator cannot invoke the spawning mechanism at all. The issue is upstream of any subagent definition.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's conversation history — context must be passed explicitly. However, this is not the cause of the failure to spawn. The fundamental issue is that the coordinator lacks the ability to invoke the Agent tool.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: There is no requirement for subagent pre-registration. Subagents are defined via AgentDefinition and spawned through the Agent tool. The issue is that the coordinator's allowedTools does not include 'Agent' (or 'Task').

exam_takeaway: The Agent tool (renamed from Task tool in SDK v2.1.63) is the mechanism for spawning subagents. If 'Agent' (or 'Task') is not in the coordinator's allowedTools, it physically cannot create subagents regardless of what the system prompt instructs. This is a configuration issue, not a prompt issue.

title: 1.4 claude-agent-sdk / multi-concern
stem: A financial services company's customer support agent receives a request: 'I was charged twice for my subscription, and I also need to update my billing address.' The agent processes the address change successfully but only partially investigates the double-charge, providing an incomplete resolution. What architectural pattern should be applied to handle this correctly?

options.A: Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to address all customer concerns before responding
options.B: Route the request to two separate specialised agents — one for billing disputes and one for address changes
options.C: Decompose the request into distinct items (double-charge investigation and address update), investigate each in parallel using shared context, and synthesise a unified resolution
options.D: Process the concerns sequentially — complete the address change first, then investigate the double-charge in a follow-up interaction

why_correct: Multi-concern request decomposition breaks the compound request into distinct items, investigates each in parallel using shared context (the customer's account), and synthesises a unified resolution that addresses all concerns. This ensures no concern is dropped or partially addressed.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Prompt-based guidance has a non-zero failure rate. Multi-concern decomposition is an architectural pattern, not a prompting issue. The agent needs a structured approach to identifying and tracking multiple concerns.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: Splitting the request across agents adds coordination overhead and may lose the shared context between the two issues. The correct pattern is multi-concern decomposition within the agent's workflow, investigating each issue in parallel with shared context.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Sequential processing across separate interactions is a poor customer experience and risks the second concern being lost. The agent should decompose, investigate in parallel, and provide a unified resolution in a single interaction.

exam_takeaway: Multi-concern request decomposition breaks the compound request into distinct items, investigates each in parallel using shared context (the customer's account), and synthesises a unified resolution that addresses all concerns. This ensures no concern is dropped or partially addressed.

sources.label: Lesson 1.4: Workflow Enforcement and Handoff (Multi-concern request handling)

title: 1.1 agentic-loops / lifecycle
stem: What value of stop_reason indicates that Claude has finished its task and no more tool calls are needed?

options.A: stop_reason='complete'
options.B: stop_reason='end_turn'
options.C: stop_reason='tool_use'
options.D: stop_reason='finished'

why_correct: When stop_reason is 'end_turn', Claude has determined it has completed its task and does not need to make any further tool calls. This is the authoritative termination signal for agentic loops.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: 'complete' is not a valid stop_reason value in the Claude API. The correct signal for task completion is 'end_turn'.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: 'tool_use' indicates the opposite — Claude wants to call a tool, meaning the loop should continue, not terminate.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: 'finished' is not a valid stop_reason value in the Claude API. The correct termination signal is 'end_turn'.

exam_takeaway: When stop_reason is 'end_turn', Claude has determined it has completed its task and does not need to make any further tool calls. This is the authoritative termination signal for agentic loops.

title: 1.1 agentic-loops / anti-patterns
stem: In an agentic loop, what is the primary role of an iteration cap?

options.A: It serves as the primary mechanism for determining when the agent has completed its task
options.B: It acts as a safety net to prevent runaway loops, not as the primary loop control mechanism
options.C: It optimises token usage by limiting the number of API calls per request
options.D: It determines the maximum number of tools the agent can call during a single iteration

why_correct: Iteration caps are safety backstops that prevent infinite loops in edge cases. The primary loop control should be stop_reason inspection. The cap catches situations where the agent gets stuck or stop_reason is never 'end_turn'.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Using an iteration cap as the primary termination mechanism is an anti-pattern. The agent may finish early (wasting iterations) or need more iterations (truncating work). The primary control should be stop_reason.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: While iteration caps do indirectly limit API calls, their purpose is safety, not optimisation. Cost control is a secondary benefit, not the primary design intent.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: An iteration cap limits the number of loop cycles, not the number of tools per cycle. Claude can call multiple tools in a single iteration. These are different concepts.

exam_takeaway: Iteration caps are safety backstops that prevent infinite loops in edge cases. The primary loop control should be stop_reason inspection. The cap catches situations where the agent gets stuck or stop_reason is never 'end_turn'.

title: 1.2 orchestration-patterns / hub-and-spoke
stem: In a hub-and-spoke orchestration pattern, how does inter-agent communication flow?

options.A: Each subagent communicates directly with every other subagent as needed
options.B: All communication flows through the coordinator — subagents never communicate directly with each other
options.C: Subagents pass results to the next agent in a predefined sequence, forming a chain
options.D: Subagents share a common message bus that all agents read from and write to

why_correct: Hub-and-spoke means the coordinator (hub) mediates all communication. Subagents (spokes) send results only to the coordinator, which then routes information to other subagents as needed. This maintains clear control flow and context management.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Direct subagent communication is a mesh pattern, not hub-and-spoke. In hub-and-spoke, subagents never communicate directly with each other.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Sequential chaining describes a pipeline pattern, not hub-and-spoke. In hub-and-spoke, the coordinator decides routing dynamically rather than following a fixed sequence.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: A shared message bus is a publish-subscribe pattern. Hub-and-spoke uses a central coordinator for all routing, not a shared bus.

exam_takeaway: Hub-and-spoke means the coordinator (hub) mediates all communication. Subagents (spokes) send results only to the coordinator, which then routes information to other subagents as needed. This maintains clear control flow and context management.

title: 1.3 guardrails-safety / posttooluse-hooks
stem: Which hook type runs after a tool has executed but before the model processes the results?

options.A: PreToolUse
options.B: PostToolUse
options.C: PreModelCall
options.D: OnToolComplete

why_correct: PostToolUse hooks run after a tool has executed and returned its results, but before those results are passed to the model for processing. This makes them ideal for normalisation, logging, and result transformation.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: PreToolUse hooks intercept tool calls before execution. They run before the tool executes, not after. Their purpose is prevention and validation of outgoing calls.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: PreModelCall is not the specific hook type for post-tool-execution processing. PostToolUse is the correct hook that intercepts results between tool execution and model processing.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: OnToolComplete is not a standard hook type in the Claude Agent SDK. The correct hook for post-execution, pre-model processing is PostToolUse.

exam_takeaway: PostToolUse hooks run after a tool has executed and returned its results, but before those results are passed to the model for processing. This makes them ideal for normalisation, logging, and result transformation.

title: 1.4 claude-agent-sdk / scoped-tools
stem: In the Claude Agent SDK, what is the purpose of the allowedTools property in an AgentDefinition?

options.A: It lists every tool available in the system so the agent knows what exists
options.B: It restricts the agent to a specific set of tools, enforcing the principle that each agent should have access to only 4–5 tools relevant to its role
options.C: It defines the order in which the agent must call its tools
options.D: It specifies which tools require human approval before execution

why_correct: allowedTools enforces scoped tool access. Each agent should only have the tools it needs for its specific role, typically 4–5 tools. This prevents agents from using tools outside their specialisation and reduces the chance of unintended actions.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: allowedTools does not catalogue the entire system's tools. It specifically restricts which tools this particular agent can access, enforcing the principle of scoped tool access.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: allowedTools does not dictate execution order. It only controls which tools the agent can access. Tool calling order is determined by the agent's reasoning within its loop.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Human approval workflows are handled by separate mechanisms, not by allowedTools. allowedTools controls tool availability, not approval requirements.

exam_takeaway: allowedTools enforces scoped tool access. Each agent should only have the tools it needs for its specific role, typically 4–5 tools. This prevents agents from using tools outside their specialisation and reduces the chance of unintended actions.

title: 1.5 multi-agent-systems / memory-isolation
stem: In a multi-agent system using the coordinator pattern, what happens to a subagent's memory when it completes its task?

options.A: The subagent's memory is automatically merged into the coordinator's context
options.B: The subagent's memory is preserved and shared with all other subagents for future reference
options.C: The subagent's internal memory is not shared — only the results it explicitly returns are available to the coordinator
options.D: The subagent's memory is stored in a global context that persists across all sessions

why_correct: Subagents do not share memory. When a subagent completes, only the explicit output it returns is passed back to the coordinator. The internal reasoning and context remain isolated and are not visible to the coordinator or other subagents, so the coordinator must pass any relevant context explicitly to subagents that need it.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Subagent memory is not automatically merged. Subagents do not share memory with the coordinator or other subagents. Only the explicit return value from the subagent's task is passed back.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: Subagents are memory-isolated. They do not share memory with each other. Each subagent has its own independent context that is not accessible to other subagents.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: There is no global persistent context shared across all subagents. Subagents are memory-isolated — each runs in its own context that is not accessible to other subagents or the coordinator.

exam_takeaway: Subagents do not share memory. When a subagent completes, only the explicit output it returns is passed back to the coordinator. The internal reasoning and context remain isolated and are not visible to the coordinator or other subagents, so the coordinator must pass any relevant context explicitly to subagents that need it.

title: 1.7 error-recovery-resilience / fork-session
stem: What is the purpose of fork_session in Claude Code?

options.A: To create a backup of the current session in case of errors
options.B: To split the current session into independent branches for divergent exploration from a shared baseline
options.C: To resume a previously terminated session from exactly where it left off
options.D: To merge the results of multiple subagents into a single output

why_correct: fork_session creates independent branches from a shared baseline. Each fork starts from the same point but can explore different approaches without contaminating each other. This is used when you want to try competing strategies from the same starting state.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: fork_session is not a backup mechanism. It creates independent exploration branches for trying different approaches from the same starting point.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Resuming a session is done with --resume, not fork_session. fork_session creates new branches, it does not resume existing sessions.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Result merging is the coordinator's responsibility. fork_session creates divergent branches; it does not merge anything.

exam_takeaway: fork_session creates independent branches from a shared baseline. Each fork starts from the same point but can explore different approaches without contaminating each other. This is used when you want to try competing strategies from the same starting state.

title: 1.6 human-in-the-loop / handoff-protocols
stem: In a structured human-in-the-loop handoff, which of the following is a required component of the escalation payload?

options.A: The full conversation transcript between the AI agent and the customer
options.B: Customer ID, conversation summary, root cause analysis, and recommended action
options.C: The AI agent's internal reasoning trace showing how it reached its conclusions
options.D: A priority score from 1–10 indicating the urgency of the escalation

why_correct: A structured handoff must include: customer ID (so the human can access the account), conversation summary (what happened), root cause analysis (why the issue occurred), refund amount if applicable, and recommended action. This makes the handoff self-contained.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: The handoff protocol assumes the human agent does NOT have access to the conversation transcript. The handoff must be self-contained with a summary, not reliant on a transcript.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Internal reasoning traces are not part of the structured handoff protocol. The human agent needs actionable information (customer ID, root cause, recommendation), not the AI's chain of thought.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Priority scoring is not part of the structured handoff protocol. The required components are customer ID, conversation summary, root cause analysis, refund amount (if applicable), and recommended action.

exam_takeaway: A structured handoff must include: customer ID (so the human can access the account), conversation summary (what happened), root cause analysis (why the issue occurred), refund amount if applicable, and recommended action. This makes the handoff self-contained.

title: 1.3 guardrails-safety / posttooluse-hooks
stem: A customer support agent must redact credit card numbers from its responses before they reach the customer. The current system prompt instructs the agent to replace card numbers with asterisks, but QA testing reveals that 6% of responses still contain unredacted card numbers. What guardrail approach should the architect use?

options.A: Rewrite the system prompt with more explicit redaction instructions and add few-shot examples of correct redaction
options.B: Implement a PostToolUse hook that applies a regex pattern to detect and redact credit card numbers from all tool results before the model processes them
options.C: Implement a PreToolUse hook that blocks any tool call containing a credit card number in its parameters
options.D: Remove all tools that might return credit card numbers from the agent's allowedTools

why_correct: A PostToolUse hook runs deterministic code (regex pattern matching) on tool results before the model sees them. This ensures credit card numbers are redacted with 100% reliability, regardless of model behaviour. This is the correct guardrail for data security requirements.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: The current prompt already instructs redaction but fails 6% of the time. Strengthening prompts may reduce the failure rate but cannot eliminate it. Leaking credit card numbers is a data security issue that demands deterministic enforcement.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: PreToolUse hooks intercept outgoing tool calls, not incoming results. The credit card numbers appear in tool results (data returned from backend systems), not in tool call parameters. PostToolUse is the correct hook type for redacting data from results.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Removing tools that return card numbers would eliminate the agent's ability to look up order and payment information, which is core to its customer support function. The correct approach is to keep the tools but redact sensitive data from their results.

exam_takeaway: A PostToolUse hook runs deterministic code (regex pattern matching) on tool results before the model sees them. This ensures credit card numbers are redacted with 100% reliability, regardless of model behaviour. This is the correct guardrail for data security requirements.

title: 1.2 orchestration-patterns / coordinator
stem: A multi-agent research system must process a customer's request that involves three sequential stages: data collection, analysis, and report generation. Each stage depends on the output of the previous one. Which orchestration pattern is most appropriate?

options.A: Parallel orchestration — run all three subagents simultaneously to minimise latency
options.B: Pipeline orchestration — pass the output of each stage as input to the next in a defined sequence
options.C: Dynamic adaptive decomposition — let the coordinator decide the order at runtime based on query complexity
options.D: Hub-and-spoke with all three agents reporting independently to the coordinator

why_correct: Pipeline orchestration is the correct pattern for sequential dependencies. Each stage completes before the next begins, with the output of one stage serving as the input to the next. This matches the data collection -> analysis -> report generation dependency chain.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Parallel execution requires independent tasks. Here, analysis depends on data collection results and report generation depends on analysis results. Running them simultaneously would mean the analysis agent has no data to analyse.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Dynamic adaptive decomposition is for open-ended investigation tasks where the next step depends on discoveries. Here, the three stages and their dependencies are known in advance, making a fixed pipeline the more predictable and efficient choice.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Independent reporting ignores the sequential dependencies. The analysis agent cannot produce meaningful results without data collection output. The pipeline must enforce the execution order.

exam_takeaway: Pipeline orchestration is the correct pattern for sequential dependencies. Each stage completes before the next begins, with the output of one stage serving as the input to the next. This matches the data collection -> analysis -> report generation dependency chain.

sources.label: Lesson 1.2: Multi-Agent Orchestration (Coordinator responsibilities)

title: 1.5 multi-agent-systems / context-passing
stem: A coordinator spawns a research subagent to investigate market trends. The subagent returns detailed findings. The coordinator then needs to pass these findings to a synthesis subagent for report writing. However, the synthesis subagent produces a report that contradicts the research findings. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The synthesis subagent has a conflicting system prompt that overrides the research data
options.B: The coordinator is passing a summary of the research findings instead of the full structured output, causing the synthesis agent to fill in gaps from its training data
options.C: The synthesis subagent has access to web search tools and is finding contradictory information online
options.D: The two subagents are using different model versions with different training data

why_correct: Subagents do not share memory. The coordinator must explicitly pass the complete research output to the synthesis agent. If the coordinator only passes a summary, the synthesis agent has no access to the detailed findings and will rely on its training data to fill gaps, potentially contradicting the actual research.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: While possible, conflicting system prompts would produce consistently wrong outputs across all requests. The more common cause is that the coordinator is not passing the full research output, so the synthesis agent fills gaps with its own training data.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: A synthesis subagent should not have web search tools — that violates scoped tool access. The synthesis agent should only have tools related to writing and formatting, not research.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Model version differences would not cause contradictions with explicitly provided research data. The issue is that the research data is not being fully passed to the synthesis agent, not that the agents have different base knowledge.

exam_takeaway: Subagents do not share memory. The coordinator must explicitly pass the complete research output to the synthesis agent. If the coordinator only passes a summary, the synthesis agent has no access to the detailed findings and will rely on its training data to fill gaps, potentially contradicting the actual research.

title: 1.3 guardrails-safety / pretooluse-hooks
stem: A developer-tool agent writes code and runs shell commands. A system prompt instruction ('Do not run destructive commands or access files outside the project') is violated 3% of the time in testing. The team requires this rule to hold absolutely. What should the architect implement?

options.A: Strengthen the system prompt with more specific examples of forbidden commands and add few-shot demonstrations
options.B: Implement PreToolUse hooks that inspect shell commands for destructive patterns and validate file paths against the project directory before execution
options.C: Implement PostToolUse hooks that detect and roll back destructive commands after they execute
options.D: Remove the shell execution tool entirely to prevent any possibility of destructive commands

why_correct: PreToolUse hooks intercept tool calls before execution. A hook can pattern-match against destructive commands like 'rm -rf' and validate that file paths fall within the project directory, blocking any violation with 100% reliability. This is deterministic enforcement for a safety-critical requirement.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: The prompt already fails 3% of the time. Strengthening it may reduce the failure rate but cannot eliminate it. Destructive operations require 100% prevention, which only deterministic enforcement can guarantee.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: PostToolUse hooks run after execution. By the time a PostToolUse hook detects 'rm -rf', the files are already deleted. Destructive commands cannot be reliably rolled back. Prevention via PreToolUse is required, not post-execution detection.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Removing shell execution eliminates the agent's ability to run any commands, including legitimate ones needed for its development workflow. The correct approach is surgical — block specific dangerous patterns while allowing legitimate usage.

exam_takeaway: PreToolUse hooks intercept tool calls before execution. A hook can pattern-match against destructive commands like 'rm -rf' and validate that file paths fall within the project directory, blocking any violation with 100% reliability. This is deterministic enforcement for a safety-critical requirement.

title: 1.4 claude-agent-sdk / scoped-tools
stem: An architect is designing a customer support system using the Claude Agent SDK. The system needs a coordinator agent that can delegate to a billing specialist and a technical support specialist. Each specialist needs different tools. How should the architect configure the AgentDefinitions?

options.A: Create one AgentDefinition with all tools from both specialists, and use prompt instructions to tell the agent which tools to use in each context
options.B: Create separate AgentDefinitions for each specialist with scoped allowedTools (4–5 tools each), and give the coordinator the Agent tool to spawn them
options.C: Create the specialists as separate API endpoints and have the coordinator call them via HTTP rather than the Agent tool
options.D: Give the coordinator all tools and have it handle all requests directly, eliminating the need for subagents

why_correct: Each specialist gets its own AgentDefinition with allowedTools restricted to the 4–5 tools relevant to its role. The coordinator has the Agent tool (renamed from Task tool in SDK v2.1.63; 'Task' still works as a backward-compatible alias) in its allowedTools so it can spawn specialists. This enforces separation of concerns and scoped tool access.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Combining all tools into one agent violates the principle of scoped tool access. With too many tools, the agent is more likely to use the wrong tool. Each specialist should have only the 4–5 tools relevant to its role.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Using HTTP calls instead of the Agent tool bypasses the Agent SDK's built-in orchestration capabilities. The Agent tool is the designed mechanism for subagent invocation and provides proper context management.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: A single agent with all tools has a higher error rate due to tool selection confusion. Specialist subagents with scoped tools produce more reliable results. The recommended maximum is 4–5 tools per agent.

exam_takeaway: Each specialist gets its own AgentDefinition with allowedTools restricted to the 4–5 tools relevant to its role. The coordinator has the Agent tool (renamed from Task tool in SDK v2.1.63; 'Task' still works as a backward-compatible alias) in its allowedTools so it can spawn specialists. This enforces separation of concerns and scoped tool access.

title: 1.7 error-recovery-resilience / fresh-start
stem: A Claude Code agent has been working on a feature branch for 45 minutes and has accumulated extensive context about the codebase. The developer notices that several tool results from early in the session (file reads from 40 minutes ago) are now stale because a colleague pushed changes to those files. The agent is making recommendations based on the outdated file contents. What is the best recovery strategy?

options.A: Continue in the current session and ask the agent to re-read the changed files
options.B: Start a completely new session with no context from the previous session
options.C: Start a fresh session with a summary injection that captures the key findings and decisions from the previous session, then read the changed files for current state
options.D: Use fork_session to create a new branch that excludes the stale tool results

why_correct: Fresh start with summary injection is the prescribed recovery strategy for stale tool results. It preserves the valuable insights and decisions from the previous session while eliminating the stale data. Reading the changed files in the new session ensures the agent works from current state.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: While re-reading files updates the information, the stale results remain in the context window. The agent may still reference the outdated content from earlier in the conversation, leading to contradictory reasoning.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: Starting fresh discards 45 minutes of accumulated context and architectural understanding. The agent would need to rediscover all the insights it already found about the codebase.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: fork_session creates a branch from the current state, which includes the stale tool results. It does not allow selective exclusion of context. It is designed for divergent exploration, not for stale context recovery.

exam_takeaway: Fresh start with summary injection is the prescribed recovery strategy for stale tool results. It preserves the valuable insights and decisions from the previous session while eliminating the stale data. Reading the changed files in the new session ensures the agent works from current state.

title: 1.6 human-in-the-loop / approval-gates
stem: A customer support agent handles account deletion requests. The company policy requires explicit human approval before any account is permanently deleted. Currently, the agent sometimes processes deletions autonomously when the customer is insistent. What approval mechanism should the architect implement?

options.A: Add a system prompt instruction: 'Always get manager approval before processing account deletions'
options.B: Implement a PreToolUse hook on the delete_account tool that pauses execution and routes the request to a human approval queue before proceeding
options.C: Remove the delete_account tool from the agent entirely and require customers to call a separate phone line
options.D: Implement a PostToolUse hook that reviews the deletion after it has been processed and reverts it if no approval was recorded

why_correct: A PreToolUse hook on the delete_account tool intercepts the call before execution and enforces the human approval requirement deterministically. The deletion cannot proceed until a human explicitly approves it, regardless of how insistent the customer is.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Prompt instructions are probabilistic. The question states the agent 'sometimes processes deletions autonomously when the customer is insistent,' showing that prompts alone are insufficient for irreversible operations that require 100% human approval.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: This creates a poor customer experience and eliminates the agent's ability to facilitate the process. The correct approach is to keep the tool but gate it behind human approval, providing a seamless escalation flow.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: PostToolUse hooks run after execution. Account deletion may be irreversible or difficult to undo. Prevention via a PreToolUse hook is required, not post-execution rollback.

exam_takeaway: A PreToolUse hook on the delete_account tool intercepts the call before execution and enforces the human approval requirement deterministically. The deletion cannot proceed until a human explicitly approves it, regardless of how insistent the customer is.

title: 1.1 agentic-loops / graceful-degradation
stem: A customer support agent's loop terminates when cumulative token usage exceeds a budget. During a complex billing investigation the budget is exhausted mid-task, after data gathering but before resolution, with stop_reason still `tool_use`. What architectural change addresses this?

options.A: Double the token budget to ensure the agent always has enough tokens to complete complex investigations
options.B: When the token budget is nearly exhausted and stop_reason is 'tool_use', trigger a graceful degradation path that summarises progress so far and escalates to a human agent with a structured handoff
options.C: Remove the token budget entirely and rely solely on the iteration cap for safety
options.D: Switch to a cheaper model to reduce token usage per iteration, allowing more iterations within the same budget

why_correct: When constraints prevent completion, the agent should degrade gracefully rather than terminating abruptly. Summarising progress and performing a structured handoff (customer ID, summary, root cause so far, recommended next steps) ensures no work is lost and the human agent can continue from where the AI left off.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Doubling the budget is an arbitrary fix that may still be insufficient for edge cases and wastes tokens on simple requests. The fundamental issue is that the budget terminates the loop even when stop_reason indicates the agent has more work to do.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Removing the token budget eliminates a valuable cost control mechanism. The issue is not having a budget, but how the system handles budget exhaustion during active work.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Using a cheaper model may reduce quality of the investigation itself. The architectural solution is graceful degradation when constraints are reached, not reducing the quality of work to fit within arbitrary limits.

exam_takeaway: When constraints prevent completion, the agent should degrade gracefully rather than terminating abruptly. Summarising progress and performing a structured handoff (customer ID, summary, root cause so far, recommended next steps) ensures no work is lost and the human agent can continue from where the AI left off.

title: 1.2 orchestration-patterns / coordinator
stem: A research coordinator spawns 4 subagents to investigate different aspects of a market analysis. Agent A fails with an API error, Agent B returns partial results (3 of 5 requested data points), and Agents C and D return complete results. The final report is due in 2 hours. What should the coordinator do?

options.A: Retry Agent A, discard Agent B's partial results, and wait for both to fully complete before proceeding
options.B: Proceed with only Agents C and D's results and produce the report without the data from Agents A and B
options.C: Retry Agent A, incorporate Agent B's partial results, flag the missing data points from B as gaps, and synthesise the report using all available results with explicit gap annotations
options.D: Terminate all agents and restart the entire investigation from scratch with a simplified scope

why_correct: The coordinator should maximise data utilisation: retry the failed agent (A), incorporate partial results from B while flagging the 2 missing data points as known gaps, and synthesise all available results from A (after retry), B (partial), C, and D. Explicit gap annotations ensure the report is transparent about its completeness.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Discarding Agent B's partial results wastes valid data. Agent B returned 3 of 5 data points, which have value. The coordinator should use what is available while attempting to fill gaps.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: This unnecessarily discards Agent B's partial results and abandons Agent A's scope entirely. A thorough coordinator should attempt recovery while incorporating all available data.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Restarting discards the complete results from Agents C and D and the partial results from Agent B. This wastes time and compute when most of the investigation has already succeeded.

exam_takeaway: The coordinator should maximise data utilisation: retry the failed agent (A), incorporate partial results from B while flagging the 2 missing data points as known gaps, and synthesise all available results from A (after retry), B (partial), C, and D. Explicit gap annotations ensure the report is transparent about its completeness.

title: 1.5 multi-agent-systems / scoped-tools
stem: A coordinator delegates to a data collection agent (`web_search`, `database_query`) and an analysis agent (`calculate`, `chart_generate`). In testing, the analysis agent calls `web_search` directly to fetch extra context, bypassing the data collection agent. What is the architectural violation and how should it be fixed?

options.A: The analysis agent's allowedTools list includes web_search, which should be removed to enforce scoped tool access. Only the data collection agent should have web_search.
options.B: Add a system prompt instruction telling the analysis agent not to use web_search even though it has access
options.C: Allow the analysis agent to keep web_search access since it sometimes needs additional context for better analysis
options.D: Implement a PostToolUse hook that logs when the analysis agent uses web_search for monitoring purposes

why_correct: Each agent should only have tools relevant to its specific role. The analysis agent should have calculate and chart_generate, not web_search. If the analysis agent needs additional data, it should request it through the coordinator, which then delegates to the data collection agent. This enforces the scoped tool access principle.

per_option_counter_explanations.B: Prompt instructions are probabilistic. The agent is already occasionally using web_search despite the architectural intent. The fix is to remove the tool from allowedTools, providing deterministic enforcement rather than hoping the prompt works.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: This violates scoped tool access and bypasses the data collection agent's role. If the analysis agent needs more data, the correct flow is: analysis agent signals the coordinator, coordinator delegates to the data collection agent, results flow back through the coordinator.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Logging the violation does not prevent it. The architectural fix is to remove web_search from the analysis agent's allowedTools, not to monitor its misuse.

exam_takeaway: Each agent should only have tools relevant to its specific role. The analysis agent should have calculate and chart_generate, not web_search. If the analysis agent needs additional data, it should request it through the coordinator, which then delegates to the data collection agent. This enforces the scoped tool access principle.

title: 1.7 error-recovery-resilience / fresh-start
stem: A CI/CD agent has spent 30 minutes debugging a failing test suite, trying three different approaches that each modified configuration files. None worked, and its context now holds three sets of conflicting modifications and failed outputs. The developer wants to try a completely different strategy. What session management approach should they use?

options.A: Continue in the current session and ask the agent to ignore all previous attempts and start fresh
options.B: Start a completely new session with no context, re-read the failing tests, and apply the new strategy
options.C: Start a fresh session with a summary injection that lists the three failed approaches and why each failed, then pursue the new strategy with clean context
options.D: Use fork_session from the point before the first debugging attempt to explore the new strategy

why_correct: Fresh start with summary injection preserves the knowledge of what has been tried (preventing repetition) while eliminating the polluted context from three sets of conflicting file modifications. The agent starts with clean context and the lessons learned from previous attempts.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Asking the agent to ignore context is unreliable. The three sets of conflicting modifications and failed outputs remain in the context window, and the model may still reason from them. This is a stale/polluted context problem.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: A completely blank session discards all the useful information about what approaches have already been tried and why they failed. This risks repeating failed approaches.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Forking from 30 minutes ago creates a branch without the knowledge of what was tried and why it failed. The new strategy benefits from knowing that three other approaches failed. Summary injection in a fresh session is more appropriate.

exam_takeaway: Fresh start with summary injection preserves the knowledge of what has been tried (preventing repetition) while eliminating the polluted context from three sets of conflicting file modifications. The agent starts with clean context and the lessons learned from previous attempts.

title: 1.6 human-in-the-loop / confidence-escalation
stem: An insurance claim agent has gathered all relevant information but the policy language admits two valid interpretations and its confidence is low. With no escalation path, the agent picks one interpretation and proceeds. What architectural improvement is needed?

options.A: Add more insurance policy documents to the agent's knowledge base to improve its interpretation accuracy
options.B: Implement a confidence threshold that triggers a structured escalation to a human claims specialist, including the customer ID, claim summary, the two possible interpretations, and supporting evidence for each
options.C: Have the agent ask the customer which interpretation they prefer
options.D: Train a fine-tuned model specifically for insurance policy interpretation

why_correct: When the agent encounters genuine ambiguity that requires human judgment, it should escalate with a structured handoff. The escalation payload includes all the information the human specialist needs: customer ID, claim summary, both interpretations, and supporting evidence. This ensures the human can make an informed decision without re-investigating.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: More documents do not resolve genuinely ambiguous policy language. When the policy itself can be read two ways, the agent needs a human expert to make the judgment call, not more reference material.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Customers cannot authoritatively interpret their own insurance policies. Policy interpretation is a specialist function that requires expertise in insurance contract language. This is a human-in-the-loop scenario requiring a specialist, not customer input.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Fine-tuning may improve accuracy but cannot guarantee correct interpretation of genuinely ambiguous language. Cases that require human judgment should escalate to human experts. The architectural fix is an escalation path, not a more specialised model.

exam_takeaway: When the agent encounters genuine ambiguity that requires human judgment, it should escalate with a structured handoff. The escalation payload includes all the information the human specialist needs: customer ID, claim summary, both interpretations, and supporting evidence. This ensures the human can make an informed decision without re-investigating.

sources.label: Lesson 1.4: Workflow Enforcement and Handoff (Confidence-based escalation)

title: 1.4 claude-agent-sdk / sequencing
stem: A coordinator using the Claude Agent SDK delegates a refactoring task to a code reviewer, a test generator, and a documentation writer in parallel, all working from the original code. The code reviewer recommends significant changes; once applied, the tests and documentation generated against the old API become invalid. What architectural fix prevents this?

options.A: Have all three agents share memory so they can see each other's outputs in real time
options.B: Use pipeline orchestration: run the code reviewer first, then pass the reviewed code to the test generator and documentation writer in parallel
options.C: Add a validation step at the end that checks whether tests and documentation match the final code
options.D: Instruct the coordinator to always run agents sequentially, one at a time, regardless of dependencies

why_correct: The code reviewer's output changes the code that tests and documentation must target. Therefore, the code reviewer must run first. Once the reviewed code is stable, the test generator and documentation writer can run in parallel since they are independent of each other. This is a hybrid pattern: sequential then parallel.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Subagents do not share memory — this is a fundamental architectural constraint. Even if they could, real-time sharing would create race conditions and ordering dependencies that are hard to manage.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Post-hoc validation detects the problem but does not prevent it. The tests and documentation must be rewritten entirely, wasting the initial parallel execution. The correct fix is to order the dependencies properly from the start.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Always sequential execution is overly conservative. The test generator and documentation writer do not depend on each other, so they can run in parallel after the code reviewer completes. The correct pattern is to parallelise independent tasks while respecting sequential dependencies.

exam_takeaway: The code reviewer's output changes the code that tests and documentation must target. Therefore, the code reviewer must run first. Once the reviewed code is stable, the test generator and documentation writer can run in parallel since they are independent of each other. This is a hybrid pattern: sequential then parallel.

sources.label: Lesson 1.4: Workflow Enforcement and Handoff (Decision rule: sequential vs parallel)
Lesson 1.2: Multi-Agent Orchestration (Coordinator responsibilities)

title: 1.5 multi-agent-systems / scoped-tools
stem: A web search agent has 9 tools: `web_search`, `url_fetch`, `html_parse`, `pdf_extract`, `image_ocr`, `translate`, `summarise`, `keyword_extract`, `sentiment_analysis`. In testing it frequently calls `summarise` and `sentiment_analysis` when it should only fetch raw data. How should the architect fix this?

options.A: Add system prompt instructions telling the web search agent to only use data fetching tools and ignore analysis tools
options.B: Reduce the web search agent's allowedTools to only the 4–5 tools relevant to data fetching (web_search, url_fetch, html_parse, pdf_extract) and move analysis tools to the appropriate specialist agents
options.C: Keep all 9 tools but implement PreToolUse hooks that block the web search agent from calling summarise and sentiment_analysis
options.D: Merge the web search and synthesis agents into a single agent since they share some tools

why_correct: The recommended maximum is 4–5 tools per agent. The web search agent has 9 tools, causing it to use tools outside its intended role. Reducing to data-fetching tools enforces scoped access. The analysis tools (summarise, sentiment_analysis, keyword_extract) belong with the synthesis or analysis agents.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Prompt instructions are probabilistic and the agent is already misusing tools. The architectural fix is to remove the tools it should not have, providing deterministic enforcement through scoped tool access.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Using hooks to block tool access is an over-engineered workaround for what should be a configuration fix. The proper solution is to remove the tools from allowedTools, not to provide them and then block their use.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Merging agents violates the principle of specialised subagents. The solution is to separate tools by role, not to combine agents. Merging would create an even larger tool set on a single agent.

exam_takeaway: The recommended maximum is 4–5 tools per agent. The web search agent has 9 tools, causing it to use tools outside its intended role. Reducing to data-fetching tools enforces scoped access. The analysis tools (summarise, sentiment_analysis, keyword_extract) belong with the synthesis or analysis agents.

sources.label: Lesson 1.4: Workflow Enforcement and Handoff (Scoped tool access (4-5 tools))
