title: 3.3 hooks-automation / skills-context-fork
stem: A documentation team creates a /generate-api-docs skill that reads source code files and produces Markdown API reference pages. The skill generates verbose output (200+ lines per endpoint) and should be available to every team member who clones the repository. How should the skill be configured?

options.A: Create a SKILL.md in ~/.claude/skills/ with context: fork frontmatter, and instruct each team member to copy it locally
options.B: Create a SKILL.md in .claude/skills/ with context: fork frontmatter so it is shared via version control and isolates verbose output from the main conversation
options.C: Add the documentation generation instructions to the root CLAUDE.md so they load automatically in every session
options.D: Create a SKILL.md in .claude/skills/ without any frontmatter, relying on the team to manually manage context overflow

why_correct: .claude/skills/ is project-scoped and version-controlled, making it available to every developer who clones the repository. context: fork isolates the verbose 200+ line output per endpoint into a forked context, preventing it from consuming the main conversation's context budget.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: ~/.claude/skills/ is user-scoped and not version-controlled. Requiring manual copying defeats the purpose of team-shared configuration and creates maintenance drift.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: CLAUDE.md is for always-loaded standards, not for on-demand command definitions. Loading verbose generation instructions in every session wastes context tokens when the team is doing non-documentation work.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Without context: fork, the verbose output (200+ lines per endpoint across many endpoints) would flood the main conversation context. The context: fork frontmatter is essential for isolating bulky output.

exam_takeaway: .claude/skills/ is project-scoped and version-controlled, making it available to every developer who clones the repository. context: fork isolates the verbose 200+ line output per endpoint into a forked context, preventing it from consuming the main conversation's context budget.

title: 3.4 permissions-security / plan-mode
stem: A documentation team must update architecture guides across 25 microservice directories after a platform migration. Each guide requires reading source, checking dependencies, and rewriting affected sections. Working in direct execution mode, a team member updates three services before noticing the results are inconsistent: some guides still mention the old platform, others use inconsistent terminology for the new one. What went wrong and what is the correct approach?

options.A: The team member should have used plan mode to establish a consistent update strategy, terminology glossary, and section-by-section template before executing changes across all 25 services
options.B: Direct execution was correct but should have been done in a single continuous session to maintain consistency through conversation context
options.C: The team member should have created a custom slash command that hardcodes the exact text replacements for each service
options.D: The team member should have used the Explore subagent to discover all affected files first, then made all changes in a single batch

why_correct: A 25-service migration with consistency requirements is a multi-step, cross-file operation where planning is essential. Plan mode would produce an explicit strategy covering terminology, update order, and validation criteria before any changes are made, preventing the inconsistency that emerged from ad hoc execution.

per_option_counter_explanations.B: A single session updating 25 services would exhaust the context window, causing later updates to lose awareness of earlier decisions. Context degradation would worsen the inconsistency problem, not solve it.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Architecture guides require contextual understanding of each service's code and dependencies — not mechanical text replacement. A slash command cannot adapt to the unique structure of each guide.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Discovery alone does not solve the consistency problem. Without an explicit plan defining terminology and update patterns, batch execution would produce the same inconsistencies faster.

exam_takeaway: A 25-service migration with consistency requirements is a multi-step, cross-file operation where planning is essential. Plan mode would produce an explicit strategy covering terminology, update order, and validation criteria before any changes are made, preventing the inconsistency that emerged from ad hoc execution.

title: 3.5 slash-commands-mcp / worktree-parallel
stem: A documentation team needs to simultaneously update API reference docs for three independent microservices after a breaking change. Each update requires reading source code, updating Markdown files, and validating links. A single Claude Code session would exhaust the context window trying to hold all three services' code simultaneously. What is the recommended approach?

options.A: Process the three services sequentially in the same session, running /compact between each service to free context
options.B: Use git worktree to create three parallel branches, each with its own Claude Code session working on one service's documentation, then merge the results
options.C: Create a single skill with context: fork that processes all three services in parallel within one session
options.D: Split the documentation files into smaller chunks and process each chunk in a separate API call using the batch API

why_correct: git worktree creates separate working directories on different branches, each with its own isolated Claude Code session. Each session has a full context budget dedicated to one service. The three updates run in parallel without interfering with each other, and results are merged via standard git workflows.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Even with /compact, each service's context (source code, documentation, edits) is substantial. Sequential processing risks context degradation as compaction summaries lose detail from earlier services, and it is slower than parallel processing.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: context: fork isolates a skill's output from the main conversation but does not create multiple parallel execution contexts. A single skill cannot simultaneously process three independent services in parallel.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: The batch API is for high-throughput, latency-tolerant workloads — not for interactive Claude Code sessions. Documentation updates require interactive exploration of source code and iterative editing, which the batch API does not support.

exam_takeaway: git worktree creates separate working directories on different branches, each with its own isolated Claude Code session. Each session has a full context budget dedicated to one service. The three updates run in parallel without interfering with each other, and results are merged via standard git workflows.

title: 3.6 cicd-integration / structured-validation
stem: A CI pipeline validates that generated API docs match the codebase. It runs `claude -p 'Verify that all public API endpoints in src/api/ have corresponding documentation in docs/api/'` with `--output-format json`. The check consistently reports 100% coverage, yet manual audits regularly find undocumented endpoints. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The --output-format json flag corrupts the analysis results, causing false positives
options.B: Claude Code is performing a surface-level pattern match rather than a deep semantic comparison, and the prompt lacks specific validation criteria and expected output structure for reporting gaps
options.C: The -p flag prevents Claude Code from reading files, so it generates a plausible-sounding report without actual file access
options.D: The CI pipeline needs a separate review step where a second Claude Code instance verifies the first instance's findings

why_correct: Without explicit validation criteria (e.g., 'for each exported function in src/api/, check that docs/api/ contains a section with the function name, parameters, and return type'), the model may perform a shallow check. Adding structured criteria, expected output format, and examples of what constitutes a gap produces reliable verification.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: --output-format json controls the output structure, not the analysis logic. It formats results as JSON for downstream parsing but does not affect the accuracy of the verification itself.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: The -p flag runs Claude Code in non-interactive (pipe) mode. It does not restrict file access — Claude Code retains full access to its built-in tools (Read, Grep, Glob) for reading files.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Adding a second instance to review the first adds latency and cost without addressing the root cause. If the first instance's prompt lacks clear validation criteria, the second instance reviewing the same vague output will draw the same flawed conclusions.

exam_takeaway: Without explicit validation criteria (e.g., 'for each exported function in src/api/, check that docs/api/ contains a section with the function name, parameters, and return type'), the model may perform a shallow check. Adding structured criteria, expected output format, and examples of what constitutes a gap produces reliable verification.

title: 3.1 configuration-settings / path-rules
stem: A docs team maintains three content types in `docs/api/`, `docs/architecture/`, and `docs/runbooks/`, each with distinct formatting, terminology, and required sections. They want Claude Code to apply the correct standards automatically when editing any docs file, without loading all three rule sets in every session. What is the correct configuration architecture?

options.A: Place all three sets of rules in the root CLAUDE.md with clear section headings so Claude Code can identify which rules apply
options.B: Create three rule files in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter paths targeting each directory: paths: ['docs/api/**'] for API rules, paths: ['docs/architecture/**'] for architecture rules, and paths: ['docs/runbooks/**'] for runbook rules
options.C: Place a separate CLAUDE.md file in each of docs/api/, docs/architecture/, and docs/runbooks/ with the type-specific rules
options.D: Create three custom skills (/api-docs, /arch-docs, /runbook-docs) and require writers to invoke the correct one before editing

why_correct: Path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ with glob patterns load only when editing files in the matching directory. Each documentation type gets its own rules loaded automatically and exclusively, conserving context tokens and eliminating the risk of applying incorrect standards.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Root CLAUDE.md loads for every session. Including all three rule sets wastes context tokens when editing only one documentation type. The model must also correctly identify which section applies, adding an unnecessary point of failure.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Directory-level CLAUDE.md files load based on the working directory hierarchy, but Claude Code sessions typically operate from the repository root. These directory-level files would only load when the agent is directly working within that specific directory, which is less reliable than path-scoped rules that match by file pattern regardless of working directory.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: This scenario explicitly requires writers to invoke the right skill manually, which depends on human memory and discipline — the wrong pick silently applies the wrong standards. Even if the skills added a paths frontmatter to auto-activate, they'd still load as a task-style workflow rather than as always-in-context guidance. Path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ are the correct choice: they load into context automatically when Claude reads a matching file, with no human step in the loop.

exam_takeaway: Path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ with glob patterns load only when editing files in the matching directory. Each documentation type gets its own rules loaded automatically and exclusively, conserving context tokens and eliminating the risk of applying incorrect standards.

title: 3.4 permissions-security / explore-subagent
stem: A documentation team member asks Claude Code to update architecture guides across 12 microservice directories. Before making any changes, they want Claude Code to first explore the codebase to understand the current state of each service. What Claude Code feature allows discovery without modification?

options.A: The Explore subagent, which delegates read-only codebase exploration to a separate context that reports findings back to the main agent
options.B: Plan mode with --dry-run flag, which simulates all file changes without writing them to disk
options.C: The allowedTools configuration set to Read and Grep only, which prevents write operations during the session
options.D: A PostToolUse hook on Write and Edit that rejects all file modifications during the exploration phase

why_correct: The Explore subagent is designed for read-only codebase discovery. It runs in a separate context, explores files and structure, and returns a summary of findings to the main agent. This preserves the main agent's context for the actual update work while gathering the necessary understanding.

per_option_counter_explanations.B: There is no --dry-run flag in Claude Code. Plan mode is for creating an execution plan before acting, but it does not provide a dedicated read-only exploration capability with separate context isolation.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: While allowedTools could restrict to read-only tools, this is a session-wide configuration change that would then need to be reversed for the update phase. The Explore subagent provides purpose-built read-only exploration without reconfiguring the session.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Hooks that reject tool calls add complexity and would need to be disabled for the update phase. The Explore subagent provides a cleaner separation between discovery and modification without hook management overhead.

exam_takeaway: The Explore subagent is designed for read-only codebase discovery. It runs in a separate context, explores files and structure, and returns a summary of findings to the main agent. This preserves the main agent's context for the actual update work while gathering the necessary understanding.

sources.label: Lesson 3.4: Plan Mode vs Direct Execution (Explore subagent)

title: 3.2 claude-md-files / hooks
stem: A documentation team wants a PostToolUse hook that automatically runs a link checker after every file write to a documentation directory. The hook should only trigger for writes to files under docs/. What determines whether a hook fires for a given tool invocation?

options.A: Hook configuration supports an `if` field that uses permission-rule syntax (e.g., "Edit(*.ts)") to match the tool name and arguments together; otherwise the hook fires for every invocation matching the `matcher`
options.B: Hooks support a `paths:` glob field in their configuration that filters which file operations trigger the hook
options.C: Hooks can be scoped to specific directories by placing the hook configuration file in that directory
options.D: Hooks fire only when the tool is invoked from a skill that has a matching paths: frontmatter

why_correct: Claude Code hooks are filtered by two configuration fields. `matcher` selects the tool name (e.g., 'Write|Edit'). `if` uses permission-rule syntax to filter on tool name and arguments together, so `Edit(*.ts)` runs only for TypeScript files and `Write(docs/**)` runs only for writes under docs/. Without an `if` field, the hook fires on every invocation that matches the matcher.

per_option_counter_explanations.B: There is no `paths:` field on hooks. Path filtering is done with the `if` field using permission-rule syntax, not a `paths:` array. The `paths:` frontmatter is used by `.claude/rules/` files, not hooks.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Hook configuration is defined in settings.json at the project or user level, not in directory-specific configuration files. Hooks do not have directory-scoped placement.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Hooks are independent of skills. They fire based on tool invocations regardless of whether those invocations originate from a skill, direct user interaction, or any other context.

exam_takeaway: Claude Code hooks are filtered by two configuration fields. `matcher` selects the tool name (e.g., 'Write|Edit'). `if` uses permission-rule syntax to filter on tool name and arguments together, so `Edit(*.ts)` runs only for TypeScript files and `Write(docs/**)` runs only for writes under docs/. Without an `if` field, the hook fires on every invocation that matches the matcher.

title: 4.1 system-prompts / false-positives
stem: Your CI/CD code review pipeline has a 40% false positive rate on 'documentation mismatch' findings, causing developers to ignore ALL review categories. What is the most effective fix?

options.A: Add 'only report high-confidence documentation issues' to the system prompt
options.B: Temporarily disable the documentation mismatch category while refining its prompts with explicit criteria and code examples
options.C: Increase the model temperature to get more varied results and filter outliers
options.D: Add a second model pass to verify each finding before reporting

why_correct: This restores trust in other categories immediately while you iterate on the problematic category with specific criteria.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Vague confidence instructions do not improve precision. The model has no concrete criteria for what 'high-confidence' means.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Temperature affects randomness, not precision. This would likely increase false positives.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: A second pass without better criteria will have the same false positive problem. Fix the criteria first.

exam_takeaway: This restores trust in other categories immediately while you iterate on the problematic category with specific criteria.

sources.label: Lesson 4.1: System Prompts with Explicit Criteria (False-positive trust problem)

title: 4.2 structured-output / few-shot-coverage
stem: Your extraction pipeline correctly identifies data in structured tables but returns empty fields when the same information appears in narrative paragraphs. Detailed instructions specify all required fields. What should you try first?

options.A: Increase the model's context window to process more of the document
options.B: Add few-shot examples showing correct extraction from both structured tables and narrative paragraphs
options.C: Add a pre-processing step to convert all narrative text into tables
options.D: Add a post-processing retry that re-extracts any empty fields

why_correct: Few-shot examples demonstrating correct handling of varied document structures directly address inconsistent extraction quality across formats.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: The model already finds data in tables. The issue is not context size but inconsistent handling of different document structures.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: This adds unnecessary complexity. The model should handle varied formats — few-shot examples teach it how.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Retrying without better guidance will produce the same empty results. The model needs examples of correct extraction from narrative text.

exam_takeaway: Few-shot examples demonstrating correct handling of varied document structures directly address inconsistent extraction quality across formats.

Lesson 4.2: Structured Output with Tool Use (What tool_use does not enforce)

title: 4.3 prompt-chaining / nullable-fields
stem: Your extraction system uses tool_use with a strict JSON schema. All fields are marked as required. Testers report that the model invents plausible-looking dates and amounts when processing documents that lack this information. What is the best fix?

options.A: Add an instruction telling the model not to hallucinate
options.B: Switch from tool_use to prompt-based JSON extraction
options.C: Make fields optional/nullable when source documents may not contain the information
options.D: Add a validation step that checks all values against the source document

why_correct: Optional/nullable fields allow the model to return null instead of fabricating values. This directly prevents fabrication for missing information.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Vague instructions do not override the schema constraint. Required fields pressure the model to produce values.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: This moves backwards in reliability. Prompt-based JSON introduces syntax errors without solving the fabrication problem.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Post-hoc validation is useful but does not address the root cause. Making fields optional prevents fabrication at the schema level.

exam_takeaway: Optional/nullable fields allow the model to return null instead of fabricating values. This directly prevents fabrication for missing information.

sources.label: Lesson 4.2: Structured Output with Tool Use (Nullable / optional fields)

title: 4.4 few-shot-examples / retry-boundary
stem: Your extraction pipeline validates that line item amounts sum to the stated total. For Document A, the sum is £450 but the stated total is £500. For Document B, the 'department' field is missing entirely from the source text. Which retry strategy is correct?

options.A: Retry both: send the validation error for Document A and instruct the model to find the missing department for Document B
options.B: Retry Document A with the discrepancy error; flag Document B for human review since the information is absent from the source
options.C: Retry both documents with the same prompt since extraction is non-deterministic
options.D: Skip retries for both and flag them for human review

why_correct: Document A has a fixable discrepancy (the model may have missed a line item). Document B has genuinely absent information — retries are ineffective.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Document B's department is absent from the source. Retrying will not make information appear that does not exist.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Non-determinism does not create information that is absent. Document A may benefit from retry; Document B will not.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Document A's discrepancy is likely fixable with error feedback. Skipping the retry wastes the model's self-correction capability.

exam_takeaway: Document A has a fixable discrepancy (the model may have missed a line item). Document B has genuinely absent information — retries are ineffective.

title: 4.5 prompt-optimisation / batch-vs-realtime
stem: Your manager proposes switching both your blocking pre-merge code review and your overnight technical debt report to the Message Batches API for 50% cost savings. How should you evaluate this proposal?

options.A: Switch both to batch processing with status polling to check for completion
options.B: Use batch processing for the technical debt reports only; keep real-time calls for pre-merge checks
options.C: Keep real-time calls for both to avoid batch result ordering issues
options.D: Switch both to batch with a timeout fallback to real-time if batches take too long

why_correct: Pre-merge checks are blocking workflows where developers wait. The batch API's 24-hour window makes it unsuitable. Technical debt reports are overnight and latency-tolerant.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Batch processing has no guaranteed latency SLA. Polling does not make it suitable for blocking pre-merge checks.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Batch results can be correlated using custom_id fields. Ordering is not the issue — latency requirements are.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: This adds unnecessary complexity. Match each API to its latency requirements: synchronous for blocking, batch for tolerant.

exam_takeaway: Pre-merge checks are blocking workflows where developers wait. The batch API's 24-hour window makes it unsuitable. Technical debt reports are overnight and latency-tolerant.

title: 4.6 output-validation / multi-pass
stem: A PR modifying 14 files receives inconsistent review: detailed feedback on some files, superficial comments on others, and contradictory findings (flagging a pattern in one file while approving identical code elsewhere). What is the best restructuring?

options.A: Switch to a higher-tier model with a larger context window
options.B: Run three independent passes on the full PR and only flag issues found in at least two passes
options.C: Split into per-file local analysis passes plus a separate cross-file integration pass
options.D: Require developers to split large PRs into smaller submissions of 3-4 files

why_correct: Per-file analysis ensures consistent depth. The integration pass catches cross-file data flow issues. This directly addresses attention dilution.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Larger context windows do not solve attention quality issues. The problem is attention dilution, not context size.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: This suppresses real bug detection by requiring consensus on issues that may only be caught intermittently.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: This shifts burden to developers without improving the review system itself.

exam_takeaway: Per-file analysis ensures consistent depth. The integration pass catches cross-file data flow issues. This directly addresses attention dilution.

title: 4.1 system-prompts / severity-examples
stem: Your Claude Code review prompt for the TypeScript monorepo classifies severity using prose descriptions like 'critical means the code is dangerous' and 'minor means the code is slightly suboptimal'. Developers complain that identical code patterns receive different severity ratings across runs. What is the most effective improvement?

options.A: Replace prose severity descriptions with concrete code examples for each severity level, showing actual TypeScript snippets that qualify as critical, major, and minor
options.B: Add a confidence threshold so only findings above 90% confidence are reported, filtering out uncertain severity ratings
options.C: Lower the model temperature to 0 to ensure deterministic severity ratings
options.D: Add a second model pass that re-evaluates each finding's severity to catch inconsistencies

why_correct: Severity calibration with concrete code examples produces consistent classification across invocations. Prose descriptions are inherently ambiguous and leave the model to interpret severity differently each time.

per_option_counter_explanations.B: Self-reported confidence scores are poorly calibrated. Confidence-based filtering does not fix the root cause, which is ambiguous severity criteria. Explicit code examples are the correct fix.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: While lower temperature reduces randomness, it does not address the fundamental problem: the model has no concrete reference for what each severity level looks like. Code examples provide that reference.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: A second pass using the same vague prose criteria will produce the same inconsistency. The criteria themselves must be improved with concrete code examples before adding verification layers.

exam_takeaway: Severity calibration with concrete code examples produces consistent classification across invocations. Prose descriptions are inherently ambiguous and leave the model to interpret severity differently each time.

sources.label: Lesson 4.1: System Prompts with Explicit Criteria (Severity calibration)

title: 4.2 structured-output / few-shot-style
stem: Your Claude Code agent generates unit tests for the TypeScript monorepo. When given detailed instructions alone, it produces tests with inconsistent assertion styles: sometimes using expect().toBe(), sometimes assert.equal(), and occasionally mixing both in the same file. Adding more detailed instructions about assertion style did not fix the problem. What should you do next?

options.A: Switch to a different model that better follows formatting instructions
options.B: Add a linter post-processing step to automatically convert all assertions to a single style
options.C: Add 2-4 few-shot examples showing complete test files with the desired assertion style and reasoning for why that style was chosen over alternatives
options.D: Add 2-4 few-shot examples demonstrating the desired assertion style with reasoning for each testing decision, covering edge cases like async functions and error handling

why_correct: Few-shot examples are the most effective technique when detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent formatting. Including 2-4 examples with reasoning teaches generalisation to novel patterns, not just pattern-matching. Covering varied scenarios (async, error handling) ensures the model generalises correctly.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: The issue is not model capability. When detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent formatting, the correct intervention is few-shot examples, not a model change.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: Post-processing masks the problem rather than solving it. The model should learn to produce consistent output directly, which few-shot examples achieve more effectively.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: This is partially correct but incomplete. The examples only cover the assertion style preference. Without covering varied scenarios (async functions, error handling), the model pattern-matches the specific cases shown rather than generalising the style consistently across all test types.

exam_takeaway: Few-shot examples are the most effective technique when detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent formatting. Including 2-4 examples with reasoning teaches generalisation to novel patterns, not just pattern-matching. Covering varied scenarios (async, error handling) ensures the model generalises correctly.

title: 4.3 prompt-chaining / tool-choice-forcing
stem: Your legal document extraction pipeline uses tool_use with tool_choice set to 'auto'. The pipeline processes contracts and sometimes receives plain text analysis instead of the structured JSON extraction you need. The team suggests switching to prompt-based JSON with explicit formatting instructions. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Switch to prompt-based JSON as suggested, since the model clearly prefers text responses for these documents
options.B: Keep tool_use but switch tool_choice from 'auto' to 'any' to guarantee the model always returns a structured tool call
options.C: Keep tool_use and set tool_choice to force the specific extraction tool, guaranteeing schema-compliant structured output on every request
options.D: Add stronger instructions in the system prompt telling the model to always use the extraction tool and never respond with plain text

why_correct: Forcing a specific tool with tool_choice {type: 'tool', name: 'extract_contract'} guarantees the model calls that exact tool every time, eliminating both text-only responses and wrong-tool selection. This is the most reliable approach for guaranteed structured output.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Prompt-based JSON is less reliable than tool_use and can produce malformed output. The issue is tool_choice configuration, not the tool_use mechanism itself.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: While 'any' guarantees a tool call, it lets the model choose which tool. If you have multiple tools defined, the model might call the wrong one. For a single extraction tool, this works, but the most precise solution is to force the specific extraction tool.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Instructions alone cannot guarantee tool use when tool_choice is 'auto'. The API-level tool_choice parameter is the correct mechanism for enforcing structured output, not prompt instructions.

exam_takeaway: Forcing a specific tool with tool_choice {type: 'tool', name: 'extract_contract'} guarantees the model calls that exact tool every time, eliminating both text-only responses and wrong-tool selection. This is the most reliable approach for guaranteed structured output.

title: 4.4 few-shot-examples / retry-with-error
stem: Your extraction pipeline retries failed documents, but the retry simply resends the original document with the same prompt. Success rates on retries are only marginally better than the first attempt. Developers have identified that most failures are format mismatches where the model places values in the wrong fields. How should you improve the retry mechanism?

options.A: Increase the number of retries from 1 to 3, since extraction is non-deterministic and more attempts improve odds
options.B: Switch to a different model for retries so a fresh perspective catches the errors
options.C: Skip retries and route all failures directly to human review to avoid wasting API costs
options.D: Send the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error (which fields had misplaced values) in the retry request

why_correct: Retry-with-error-feedback is dramatically more effective than naive retries. Sending the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error allows the model to self-correct. Format mismatches are fixable errors that respond well to this approach.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Naive retries without error feedback produce the same mistakes. More attempts at the same flawed approach yield diminishing returns. The model needs to see what went wrong.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: The issue is not the model but the absence of error context. Any model retrying without seeing the specific validation error will likely repeat the same mistakes.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Format mismatches are fixable errors. The model can self-correct when given proper error feedback. Skipping retries wastes the model's self-correction capability for errors that are resolvable.

exam_takeaway: Retry-with-error-feedback is dramatically more effective than naive retries. Sending the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error allows the model to self-correct. Format mismatches are fixable errors that respond well to this approach.

title: 4.5 prompt-optimisation / batch-failure
stem: Your CI/CD pipeline generates nightly security audit reports using the Message Batches API. A batch of 200 documents completes overnight, but 15 documents fail due to exceeding the context window. The team proposes resubmitting the entire batch of 200 documents. What is the correct failure handling strategy?

options.A: Resubmit the entire batch since you cannot identify which documents failed
options.B: Resubmit only the 15 failed documents identified by custom_id, chunking the oversized documents before resubmission
options.C: Switch the entire pipeline to synchronous processing to avoid batch failures
options.D: Increase the batch processing timeout to give the system more time to handle large documents

why_correct: Identify failed documents by custom_id, then resubmit only failures with modifications (chunking oversized documents). This is the correct batch failure handling pattern — it avoids reprocessing the 185 successful documents and addresses the root cause of the failures.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: The batch API uses custom_id fields to correlate request/response pairs. Failed documents can be identified by their custom_id, making full resubmission unnecessary and wasteful.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Nightly security audits are latency-tolerant workloads perfectly suited for batch processing. Switching to synchronous forfeits the 50% cost savings without solving the oversized document problem.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: The failure is due to documents exceeding the context window, not a timeout issue. The documents need to be chunked to fit within the model's context limits.

exam_takeaway: Identify failed documents by custom_id, then resubmit only failures with modifications (chunking oversized documents). This is the correct batch failure handling pattern — it avoids reprocessing the 185 successful documents and addresses the root cause of the failures.

title: 4.6 output-validation / self-review-bias
stem: Your Claude Code setup reviews generated code by asking the same model instance to critique its own output immediately after generation, within the same conversation. The team notices the reviews are overly favourable and miss bugs that an external reviewer would catch. What is the root cause and correct fix?

options.A: The model needs more detailed review instructions; add a comprehensive checklist of what to look for during self-review
options.B: Enable extended thinking so the model reasons more carefully about potential issues in its own code
options.C: The model retains reasoning context from generation; use a separate independent Claude instance without the prior conversation context to perform the review
options.D: Lower the temperature during the review phase to make the model more precise and less likely to approve questionable code

why_correct: A model reviewing its own output in the same session retains reasoning context and is less likely to question its own decisions. An independent instance without prior context catches more subtle issues because it approaches the code fresh.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: More detailed instructions do not overcome the fundamental limitation. The model retains its reasoning context from generation and is less likely to question its own decisions regardless of how detailed the checklist is.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: Extended thinking does not solve the self-review limitation. The model still retains its reasoning context and is biased towards its own output. Extended thinking makes the existing reasoning deeper, not more independent.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Temperature affects response variability, not the fundamental bias of self-review. The model will still be biased towards its own output regardless of temperature settings. An independent instance is the correct architectural fix.

exam_takeaway: A model reviewing its own output in the same session retains reasoning context and is less likely to question its own decisions. An independent instance without prior context catches more subtle issues because it approaches the code fresh.

title: 4.1 system-prompts / severity-examples
stem: When writing system prompts for Claude Code to classify code review findings by severity, which approach produces the most consistent classification across repeated invocations?

options.A: Prose descriptions of each severity level, such as 'critical issues are dangerous to production'
options.B: Concrete code examples for each severity level, showing actual snippets that qualify as critical, major, and minor
options.C: A numerical scoring rubric from 1 to 10 with threshold ranges for each severity level
options.D: A decision tree with yes/no questions that the model follows to determine severity

why_correct: Concrete code examples provide an unambiguous reference for each severity level. The model matches incoming code against these examples rather than interpreting vague prose, producing consistent classification.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Prose descriptions are inherently ambiguous. Different invocations interpret words like 'dangerous' and 'suboptimal' differently, leading to inconsistent severity ratings.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Numerical scores still require the model to interpret what constitutes a '7' versus an '8'. Without concrete examples, this is just prose descriptions with numbers attached.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Decision trees can help but still rely on subjective interpretation at each branch point. Concrete code examples are more effective because they directly show the model what each severity level looks like.

exam_takeaway: Concrete code examples provide an unambiguous reference for each severity level. The model matches incoming code against these examples rather than interpreting vague prose, producing consistent classification.

title: 4.2 structured-output / tool-use-vs-prompt-json
stem: Why does using tool_use for structured output provide stronger guarantees than prompt-based JSON extraction?

options.A: tool_use is faster because the model skips generating natural language tokens
options.B: tool_use enforces schema compliance, guaranteeing the output matches the defined structure, whereas prompt-based JSON risks syntax errors and missing fields
options.C: tool_use costs less per token than prompt-based extraction
options.D: tool_use can extract data that prompt-based JSON cannot access in the source document

why_correct: tool_use validates output against a predefined schema, ensuring all required fields are present and correctly typed. Prompt-based JSON relies on the model to remember and follow formatting rules, which can produce malformed output, missing brackets, or omitted fields.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: tool_use does not inherently improve speed. Its advantage is schema compliance, not latency.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Pricing is not the differentiator. The advantage of tool_use is guaranteed schema compliance, not cost.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Both approaches have access to the same source content. tool_use does not grant additional data access; it guarantees the output structure.

exam_takeaway: tool_use validates output against a predefined schema, ensuring all required fields are present and correctly typed. Prompt-based JSON relies on the model to remember and follow formatting rules, which can produce malformed output, missing brackets, or omitted fields.

title: 4.4 few-shot-examples / how-many
stem: What is the recommended number of few-shot examples to include when guiding Claude's output format, and what should those examples contain?

options.A: 1 example showing the ideal output format without explanation
options.B: 2-4 examples with reasoning, covering varied scenarios including edge cases
options.C: 8-10 examples covering every possible edge case to maximise coverage
options.D: 2-4 examples showing only the correct output, without reasoning or edge cases

why_correct: 2-4 examples with reasoning is the recommended range. Including reasoning teaches the model why each decision was made, enabling generalisation. Covering varied scenarios (such as async functions and error handling) prevents the model from pattern-matching only the specific cases shown.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: A single example risks the model overfitting to that specific case rather than generalising the pattern. Without reasoning, the model cannot distinguish which aspects of the example are important.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Too many examples consume context window space and can cause the model to overfit to the examples rather than generalise. 2-4 well-chosen examples with reasoning are more effective.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: The correct number of examples is right, but omitting reasoning and edge cases limits effectiveness. The model needs reasoning to generalise and edge cases to handle varied inputs.

exam_takeaway: 2-4 examples with reasoning is the recommended range. Including reasoning teaches the model why each decision was made, enabling generalisation. Covering varied scenarios (such as async functions and error handling) prevents the model from pattern-matching only the specific cases shown.

title: 4.5 prompt-optimisation / batch-tradeoff
stem: What is the primary cost benefit of the Message Batches API, and what is the trade-off?

options.A: 25% cost reduction with a guaranteed 1-hour processing window
options.B: 50% cost reduction with a 24-hour processing window, suitable only for latency-tolerant workloads
options.C: 50% cost reduction with guaranteed sub-minute response times for each item in the batch
options.D: 75% cost reduction with a 48-hour processing window

why_correct: The Batches API offers 50% cost savings but processes within a 24-hour window with no guaranteed latency SLA. This makes it suitable only for workloads where immediate results are not needed, such as overnight reports or bulk analysis.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: The cost reduction is 50%, not 25%, and the processing window is 24 hours, not 1 hour.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: The Batches API does not guarantee sub-minute responses. The trade-off is specifically the lack of latency guarantees within the 24-hour window.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: The cost reduction is 50% and the processing window is 24 hours. These figures are defined in the Batches API specification.

exam_takeaway: The Batches API offers 50% cost savings but processes within a 24-hour window with no guaranteed latency SLA. This makes it suitable only for workloads where immediate results are not needed, such as overnight reports or bulk analysis.

title: 4.6 output-validation / self-review-bias
stem: Why does asking Claude to review its own output within the same conversation session produce unreliable reviews?

options.A: The model has a hard-coded limit on how many issues it can identify per session
options.B: The model's context window fills up, leaving insufficient space for review analysis
options.C: The model retains its reasoning context from generation and is biased towards its own decisions, making it less likely to identify flaws
options.D: The model's temperature setting resets to a higher value during review, producing less precise analysis

why_correct: A model reviewing its own output in the same session retains the reasoning that led to its original decisions. This creates a confirmation bias where the model is less likely to question choices it already justified to itself.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: There is no hard-coded limit on identified issues. The problem is cognitive bias from retained reasoning context, not a technical constraint.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: Context window exhaustion is a separate concern. Self-review bias occurs even when ample context remains because the model retains its original reasoning.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Temperature does not reset between turns. The issue is reasoning bias from the shared session context, not temperature settings.

exam_takeaway: A model reviewing its own output in the same session retains the reasoning that led to its original decisions. This creates a confirmation bias where the model is less likely to question choices it already justified to itself.

title: 4.3 prompt-chaining / inter-step-validation
stem: In a multi-step prompt chain, what should happen between each step to maintain pipeline reliability?

options.A: Each step's output should be passed directly to the next step without interruption to maintain conversational flow
options.B: Validation should occur between steps, checking that each step's output meets the expected format and content requirements before proceeding
options.C: The entire chain should run in a single API call to minimise latency and cost
options.D: A human reviewer should approve each intermediate output before the chain continues

why_correct: Inter-step validation catches errors early, preventing cascading failures. Each step should produce focused output that is validated before the next step consumes it. This is a core principle of reliable prompt chaining.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Passing output directly without validation risks cascading errors. A malformed output from step 1 corrupts all downstream steps.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Combining all steps in a single call eliminates the ability to validate between steps and creates attention dilution. Separate focused steps with validation are more reliable.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Human-in-the-loop at every step defeats the purpose of automation. Programmatic validation between steps is the correct approach for production pipelines.

exam_takeaway: Inter-step validation catches errors early, preventing cascading failures. Each step should produce focused output that is validated before the next step consumes it. This is a core principle of reliable prompt chaining.

title: 4.1 system-prompts / keyword-overlap
stem: Your CI/CD pipeline uses a system prompt with a tool named 'check_security' and also includes instructions that say 'check the security of each function'. Developers report that the model sometimes produces a text-based security analysis instead of calling the check_security tool. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The model's temperature is too high, causing random tool selection
options.B: Keyword overlap between the instruction text 'check the security' and the tool name 'check_security' causes the model to confuse instruction-following with tool invocation
options.C: The model cannot call tools from within a CI/CD pipeline context
options.D: The system prompt is too long, causing the model to skip tool definitions

why_correct: When system prompt instructions use phrasing that closely mirrors tool names, the model can interpret 'check the security' as a general instruction rather than a trigger for the check_security tool. Distinct naming reduces this ambiguity.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Temperature affects randomness in generation but is not the primary cause of tool call confusion. The issue is prompt design, not sampling parameters.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Tool calling works in any context. The issue is prompt design, not an environmental limitation.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: System prompt length does not cause tool definitions to be skipped. The model processes tools and instructions together. The issue is keyword overlap creating ambiguity.

exam_takeaway: When system prompt instructions use phrasing that closely mirrors tool names, the model can interpret 'check the security' as a general instruction rather than a trigger for the check_security tool. Distinct naming reduces this ambiguity.

stem: Your data extraction pipeline uses tool_use with tool_choice set to 'auto'. You need guaranteed structured output for every request, but some documents occasionally produce conversational text responses instead. You have only one extraction tool defined. What is the most reliable fix?

options.B: Set tool_choice to force the specific extraction tool by name
options.C: Add a post-processing step that retries any request returning text instead of a tool call

per_option_counter_explanations.A: System prompt instructions cannot guarantee tool use when tool_choice is 'auto'. The API-level tool_choice parameter is the authoritative mechanism.

per_option_counter_explanations.D: Prompt-based JSON is less reliable than tool_use. It risks syntax errors and missing fields. Forcing the tool via tool_choice is the correct approach.

title: 4.3 prompt-chaining / inter-step-validation
stem: Your document processing pipeline chains three steps: (1) extract raw text, (2) classify document type, (3) extract structured fields based on type. Step 2 occasionally misclassifies invoices as purchase orders, causing step 3 to extract the wrong fields. The team proposes combining steps 2 and 3 into a single prompt to reduce errors. What is the better approach?

options.A: Combine steps 2 and 3 as proposed, since fewer steps means fewer failure points
options.B: Keep the steps separate but add validation between steps 2 and 3 that checks classification confidence and routes low-confidence documents for re-classification before extraction
options.C: Add more document type examples to step 2's prompt to improve classification accuracy
options.D: Run step 2 three times and use majority voting to determine the document type

why_correct: Keeping steps separate maintains focused prompts. Adding validation between steps catches misclassifications before they cascade into wrong-field extraction. This is the core principle of prompt chaining: focused steps with inter-step validation.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Combining steps creates a less focused prompt that must handle both classification and extraction simultaneously. This increases attention dilution and makes it harder to diagnose which part fails.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Better examples may help, but without validation between steps, misclassifications still cascade silently into step 3. Inter-step validation is the structural fix.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Majority voting adds cost and latency without addressing the root cause. Validation between steps is more efficient and catches the specific failure mode.

exam_takeaway: Keeping steps separate maintains focused prompts. Adding validation between steps catches misclassifications before they cascade into wrong-field extraction. This is the core principle of prompt chaining: focused steps with inter-step validation.

title: 4.4 few-shot-examples / construction
stem: Your Claude Code agent generates API endpoint implementations. You provide detailed instructions specifying error handling conventions, but the generated code inconsistently handles async errors: sometimes using try/catch, sometimes using .catch(), and sometimes omitting error handling entirely. Adding more detailed instructions did not resolve the inconsistency. What is the most effective next step?

options.A: Add a linting rule to catch missing error handling and reject generated code that fails the lint
options.B: Add 2-4 few-shot examples demonstrating the correct error handling pattern across varied scenarios, including async/await, Promise chains, and edge cases, with reasoning for each choice

why_correct: When detailed instructions alone fail to produce consistent formatting, few-shot examples with reasoning are the correct escalation. Covering varied async scenarios prevents the model from pattern-matching only the specific cases shown and teaches it to generalise the error handling style.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Linting can catch missing error handling but does not address the inconsistent style (try/catch versus .catch()). The model needs to see the desired pattern demonstrated, not just be told about it.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Temperature does not fix ambiguous criteria. If the instructions do not clearly demonstrate the preferred pattern, low temperature just makes the model consistently pick the same ambiguous interpretation, not necessarily the correct one.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Post-processing adds cost and complexity. It is more effective to teach the model the correct pattern upfront with few-shot examples than to fix incorrect output afterwards.

exam_takeaway: When detailed instructions alone fail to produce consistent formatting, few-shot examples with reasoning are the correct escalation. Covering varied async scenarios prevents the model from pattern-matching only the specific cases shown and teaches it to generalise the error handling style.

title: 4.5 prompt-optimisation / custom-id
stem: Your CI/CD pipeline processes code reviews using the Message Batches API. After a batch completes, you need to match each review result back to the corresponding pull request. What is the correct mechanism for correlating batch results with their original requests?

options.A: Parse the review content to identify which pull request it refers to based on file names mentioned in the review

options.C: Use the custom_id field in each batch request to store the pull request identifier, then match results by custom_id

per_option_counter_explanations.D: Submitting individual batches defeats the purpose of batch processing and does not leverage the custom_id mechanism designed for exactly this use case.

title: 4.6 output-validation / multi-pass
stem: Your CI/CD code review system analyses pull requests averaging 8-12 files. Reviews are thorough on the first few files but become increasingly superficial on later files, sometimes missing obvious issues. What architectural change best addresses this pattern?

options.A: Randomise the file order before each review so different files get thorough treatment
options.B: Increase the model's context window to give it more space to analyse all files
options.C: Split the review into per-file analysis passes where each file gets dedicated attention, followed by a cross-file integration pass for inter-file concerns
options.D: Add a second full-PR review pass and merge findings from both passes

why_correct: Per-file analysis ensures each file receives consistent, thorough attention. The cross-file integration pass then catches issues that span multiple files, such as inconsistent interfaces or data flow problems. This directly solves attention dilution.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Randomising order means different files get superficial treatment each time, but does not ensure all files receive thorough review. The root cause — attention dilution — remains.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: Attention dilution is not a context window size problem. The model has enough space but distributes attention unevenly across many files.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: A second pass on the full PR suffers from the same attention dilution. Both passes will likely be thorough on early files and superficial on later ones.

exam_takeaway: Per-file analysis ensures each file receives consistent, thorough attention. The cross-file integration pass then catches issues that span multiple files, such as inconsistent interfaces or data flow problems. This directly solves attention dilution.

title: 4.5 prompt-optimisation / prompt-caching
stem: When using prompt caching to optimise a pipeline that processes many documents with the same extraction instructions, where should the static and dynamic content be placed in the prompt?

options.A: Dynamic document content at the beginning, static extraction instructions at the end
options.B: Static extraction instructions at the beginning, dynamic document content at the end
options.C: Interleave static instructions and dynamic content throughout the prompt for better context
options.D: Put all content in a single message with no particular ordering, since prompt caching automatically identifies cacheable sections

why_correct: Prompt caching caches a prefix of the prompt. Placing static content (extraction instructions, few-shot examples, schema definitions) at the beginning means this prefix is cached and reused across all document requests. Dynamic content (the document being processed) goes at the end.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: This is the reverse of the correct order. Prompt caching works by caching a prefix. If dynamic content comes first, the prefix changes with every request, defeating the cache entirely.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Interleaving breaks the static prefix, preventing effective caching. The cache requires a contiguous block of static content at the start.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Prompt caching does not automatically identify cacheable sections. It caches a prefix, so you must deliberately structure the prompt with static content first.

exam_takeaway: Prompt caching caches a prefix of the prompt. Placing static content (extraction instructions, few-shot examples, schema definitions) at the beginning means this prefix is cached and reused across all document requests. Dynamic content (the document being processed) goes at the end.

title: 4.1 system-prompts / keyword-overlap
stem: A CI/CD system prompt defines two review categories with the instructions 'Check for security vulnerabilities in each function' and 'Check for performance issues in each loop'. The model frequently calls `performance_check` for security issues found inside loops, and `security_check` for performance issues in security-sensitive functions. What is the root cause and best fix?

options.A: The model is confused because loops can have both security and performance issues; add a rule that security always takes priority over performance
options.B: Keyword overlap between instruction phrasing and tool names causes the model to associate 'loop' with performance and 'function' with security regardless of the actual issue; rewrite instructions and tool descriptions to use distinct, non-overlapping terminology
options.C: Add more detailed tool descriptions explaining exactly when each tool should be called
options.D: Force tool_choice to 'auto' and let the model determine the correct tool based on the content of each finding

why_correct: When instruction text like 'check for security in each function' overlaps with tool name patterns, the model conflates instruction keywords with tool selection cues. Using distinct terminology for instructions versus tool names eliminates this cross-contamination.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Priority rules add complexity without fixing the root cause. The model is confusing tools because the instruction keywords overlap with both tool names and each other.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: More detailed descriptions help but do not fix the root cause if the instruction text still contains overlapping keywords that cue the wrong tool.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: tool_choice 'auto' is likely already the setting. The problem is that the model's tool selection is being misled by keyword overlap in the prompt, not by the tool_choice configuration.

exam_takeaway: When instruction text like 'check for security in each function' overlaps with tool name patterns, the model conflates instruction keywords with tool selection cues. Using distinct terminology for instructions versus tool names eliminates this cross-contamination.

title: 4.2 structured-output / nullable-fields
stem: An extraction pipeline uses `tool_use` with a 15-required-field schema. For some document types, only 8 of those fields ever appear in the source material. The model consistently fabricates plausible values for the missing 7, and the instruction 'do not fabricate data' has not helped. Should the team (A) keep all fields required and add post-extraction validation, or (B) redesign the schema? Which is correct and why?

options.A: Keep all fields required and add post-extraction validation to detect and remove fabricated values
options.B: Redesign the schema to make the 7 sometimes-absent fields optional/nullable, allowing the model to return null instead of fabricating
options.C: Create separate schemas for each document type, each containing only the fields present in that document type
options.D: Switch to prompt-based JSON extraction where you can instruct the model to omit absent fields entirely

why_correct: Making fields optional/nullable when source data may be absent removes the schema-level pressure to fabricate. The model can legitimately return null for missing information, which is a correct representation of reality. This addresses the root cause at the schema level.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Post-extraction validation cannot reliably distinguish fabricated values from correct ones — fabricated values are designed to look plausible. The schema itself forces fabrication by making all fields required.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Multiple schemas add maintenance complexity and require document type classification before extraction. Making fields nullable in a single schema is simpler and equally effective.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Prompt-based JSON sacrifices schema compliance guarantees. tool_use with optional fields gives both flexibility for absent data and schema validation for present data.

exam_takeaway: Making fields optional/nullable when source data may be absent removes the schema-level pressure to fabricate. The model can legitimately return null for missing information, which is a correct representation of reality. This addresses the root cause at the schema level.

title: 4.3 prompt-chaining / attention-dilution
stem: An extraction pipeline processes 50-page legal contracts in a single API call. It captures parties and dates from the first few pages but misses key financial terms in later pages, and occasionally contradicts itself across fields. A colleague suggests simply increasing the context window. What is the correct diagnosis and fix?

options.A: The context window is too small; upgrading to a larger context model will fix the inconsistency
options.B: This is attention dilution; split into per-section extraction passes for each document area followed by a cross-section integration pass that reconciles and validates the combined output
options.C: Run the full extraction three times and take the most common value for each field
options.D: Add more detailed instructions about the importance of financial terms to increase the model's focus on those sections

why_correct: Long documents cause attention dilution: the model attends thoroughly to early content but loses focus on later sections. Per-section passes ensure each part gets dedicated attention, and the integration pass catches contradictions and reconciles fields across sections.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: If the document fits in the context window, a larger window does not improve attention quality. The problem is attention dilution over a long document, not context capacity.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Multiple passes on the full document suffer from the same attention dilution pattern. The model will repeatedly extract early-page data well and miss later-page data.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Instructions cannot override the attention dilution effect of processing a 50-page document in one pass. The structural fix is breaking the extraction into focused per-section passes.

exam_takeaway: Long documents cause attention dilution: the model attends thoroughly to early content but loses focus on later sections. Per-section passes ensure each part gets dedicated attention, and the integration pass catches contradictions and reconciles fields across sections.

title: 4.5 prompt-optimisation / prompt-caching
stem: Your Claude Code setup uses a complex system prompt with detailed review instructions, code examples, and few-shot demonstrations that total 4,000 tokens. Each code review request adds 500-2,000 tokens of code to review. The team wants to optimise costs since the same review instructions are used for every request. What is the most effective optimisation?

options.A: Shorten the system prompt by removing few-shot examples to reduce per-request token costs
options.B: Enable prompt caching with the static review instructions and examples at the beginning of the prompt, placing the dynamic code-to-review at the end
options.C: Switch all code reviews to the Message Batches API for 50% cost savings
options.D: Reduce the number of few-shot examples from 4 to 1 and lower the temperature to compensate for the reduced guidance

why_correct: Prompt caching caches the static prefix and reuses it across requests. With 4,000 tokens of static content reused for every review, caching provides significant cost savings without sacrificing review quality. Dynamic code goes at the end so the prefix remains cacheable.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Removing few-shot examples degrades review quality. The 4,000-token static prompt is the ideal candidate for caching, not trimming.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Code reviews in Claude Code are interactive, blocking workflows. The Batches API's 24-hour window makes it unsuitable for developer-facing reviews.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Lower temperature does not compensate for reduced examples. Fewer examples degrade quality. Prompt caching preserves the full prompt while reducing costs.

exam_takeaway: Prompt caching caches the static prefix and reuses it across requests. With 4,000 tokens of static content reused for every review, caching provides significant cost savings without sacrificing review quality. Dynamic code goes at the end so the prefix remains cacheable.

title: 4.6 output-validation / retry-with-error
stem: Your extraction pipeline has a validation step that checks extracted financial data. When validation fails, the system retries by sending just the original document with the same prompt. Retry success rates are below 10%. The most common failure is the model placing the 'net amount' value in the 'gross amount' field and vice versa. How should the retry be restructured?

options.A: Increase retries from 1 to 5, since more attempts at the same prompt will eventually produce the correct field mapping by chance
options.B: Send the original document, the failed extraction output, and the specific validation error explaining which fields were swapped, so the model can self-correct
options.C: Add a post-processing rule that automatically swaps net and gross amounts when validation detects the pattern
options.D: Switch to a different model for the retry, since the original model has a persistent field-mapping bias

why_correct: Retry-with-error-feedback is dramatically more effective than naive retries. The model seeing its specific mistake (net and gross amounts swapped) and the validation error allows targeted self-correction rather than repeating the same misinterpretation.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: If the model consistently maps fields incorrectly with the same prompt, more retries without feedback will produce the same incorrect mapping. The model needs to see its specific error.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Hard-coded swap rules are brittle and mask the underlying extraction error. They also fail if the issue manifests differently in other documents. Error feedback teaches the model to extract correctly.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: The issue is the absence of error context in the retry, not a model-specific bias. Any model retrying without seeing the specific validation error will have a low success rate.

exam_takeaway: Retry-with-error-feedback is dramatically more effective than naive retries. The model seeing its specific mistake (net and gross amounts swapped) and the validation error allows targeted self-correction rather than repeating the same misinterpretation.

title: 4.1 system-prompts / explicit-criteria
stem: The moderation system's prompt instructs Claude to 'be conservative when moderating and err on the side of caution.' Reviewers find that innocuous posts about cooking with knives, news articles about violence, and fictional war stories are all being flagged as policy violations. What is the root cause and fix?

options.A: The model is too sensitive — lower the temperature to reduce over-flagging
options.B: Replace 'be conservative' with explicit categorical criteria — define each violation category with specific indicators, severity levels, and concrete examples of what does and does not qualify, including edge cases like news reporting and fiction
options.C: Add an allowlist of safe topics (cooking, news, fiction) that should never be flagged
options.D: Add a second pass that reviews flagged posts and removes false positives before actioning them

why_correct: Vague directives like 'be conservative' give the model no basis for distinguishing between genuine violations and legitimate content that mentions sensitive topics. Explicit criteria with examples of both violations and non-violations (news, fiction, educational content) enable consistent, calibrated decisions.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Temperature affects randomness, not the interpretation of moderation criteria. The over-flagging is caused by vague instructions, not sampling behaviour.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Allowlists are brittle and impossible to maintain comprehensively. New safe topics will constantly appear. The fix is better criteria that teach the model to distinguish context, not a growing list of exceptions.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: A second pass using the same vague 'be conservative' criteria will reproduce the same false positives. Fix the criteria first; add verification layers second.

exam_takeaway: Vague directives like 'be conservative' give the model no basis for distinguishing between genuine violations and legitimate content that mentions sensitive topics. Explicit criteria with examples of both violations and non-violations (news, fiction, educational content) enable consistent, calibrated decisions.

title: 4.1 system-prompts / severity-examples
stem: A moderation team introduces a severity scale ('low', 'medium', 'high', 'critical'). The same post (a user threatening to 'destroy' a competitor's product in a review) is classified as 'high' on some runs and 'low' on others. The prompt defines severities with phrases like 'high means the content is clearly harmful' and 'low means the content is mildly inappropriate'. What should they change?

options.A: Set temperature to 0 to eliminate classification variance across runs
options.B: Replace prose severity descriptions with concrete examples for each level — 'high' includes direct threats of physical harm with specifics; 'low' includes figurative language in product reviews — so the model has calibration anchors for each severity
options.C: Remove the severity scale and use binary classification (violation / not violation) to reduce inconsistency
options.D: Run the classification three times and take the majority vote for severity

why_correct: Concrete examples anchor each severity level to specific, observable patterns. When the model sees 'destroy a competitor's product' in a review context, it can match against the 'low severity — figurative language' example rather than interpreting 'clearly harmful' differently each run.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Lower temperature reduces randomness but does not fix ambiguous criteria. The model is inconsistent because the severity definitions are vague, not because of sampling variance.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Binary classification loses valuable granularity needed for routing decisions (auto-remove vs escalate vs warn). The fix is better severity criteria, not removing severity entirely.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Majority voting averages out noise but triples cost and latency without fixing the root cause. With vague criteria, the model may consistently misclassify in the same direction, making voting ineffective.

exam_takeaway: Concrete examples anchor each severity level to specific, observable patterns. When the model sees 'destroy a competitor's product' in a review context, it can match against the 'low severity — figurative language' example rather than interpreting 'clearly harmful' differently each run.

sources.label: Lesson 4.1: System Prompts with Explicit Criteria (Severity calibration)

title: 4.2 structured-output / few-shot-coded-content
stem: The moderation system classifies hate speech accurately for explicit slurs but misses coded language and dog-whistle terms that human moderators easily recognise. The prompt includes detailed written rules about coded language patterns. What intervention would most improve detection of coded hate speech?

options.A: Add a comprehensive dictionary of all known coded terms and dog-whistles to the system prompt
options.B: Add 2-4 few-shot examples showing coded hate speech alongside the reasoning that identifies the coded language, the targeted group, and why the surface text appears innocuous
options.C: Add 20+ examples covering every known category of coded hate speech to maximise coverage
options.D: Increase the model's context window so it can consider more of the user's post history for context

why_correct: Few-shot examples with reasoning tags teach the model the pattern-recognition process, not just individual terms. Showing the reasoning chain — surface meaning, coded meaning, targeted group, contextual signals — enables the model to generalise to new coded terms it has not seen before.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: A static dictionary becomes outdated immediately as coded language constantly evolves. It also bloats the prompt without teaching the model to recognise the underlying patterns of coded speech.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Laundry lists of examples dilute attention and teach pattern-matching rather than generalisation. 2-4 targeted examples with reasoning are more effective than 20 examples without reasoning because they teach the analytical process.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Context window size is not the bottleneck. The model fails to recognise coded language in individual posts, which is a prompt engineering issue, not a context limitation.

exam_takeaway: Few-shot examples with reasoning tags teach the model the pattern-recognition process, not just individual terms. Showing the reasoning chain — surface meaning, coded meaning, targeted group, contextual signals — enables the model to generalise to new coded terms it has not seen before.

sources.label: Lesson 4.4: Few-Shot Prompting (Few-shot for nuanced detection)

title: 4.2 structured-output / few-shot-ambiguity
stem: The moderation team is designing few-shot examples to teach Claude how to handle ambiguous content — posts that could be either satirical commentary or genuine policy violations depending on context. What is the recommended approach for structuring these few-shot examples?

options.A: Provide examples of clear violations and clear non-violations only, avoiding ambiguous cases to prevent confusion
options.B: Include 2-4 targeted examples that demonstrate ambiguous-case handling, with reasoning tags explaining how context, tone, and intent distinguish satire from genuine violations
options.C: Provide 15-20 examples covering every possible type of satire to ensure comprehensive coverage
options.D: Provide examples showing only the correct classification label without reasoning, so the model focuses on the output format

why_correct: Few-shot examples should target the failure mode. Including ambiguous cases with explicit reasoning chains teaches the model to evaluate context, tone, and intent — the exact signals needed to distinguish satire from genuine violations.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Avoiding ambiguous cases in examples leaves the model without guidance for precisely the scenarios that cause the most classification errors. Ambiguous cases need explicit demonstration.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Large numbers of examples dilute the model's attention and teach surface-level pattern matching. 2-4 well-reasoned examples that demonstrate the analytical process generalise better than an exhaustive list.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Examples without reasoning teach the model what to output but not how to decide. For ambiguous cases, the reasoning process is essential — the model needs to learn how to weigh context signals, not just memorise label mappings.

exam_takeaway: Few-shot examples should target the failure mode. Including ambiguous cases with explicit reasoning chains teaches the model to evaluate context, tone, and intent — the exact signals needed to distinguish satire from genuine violations.
