title: 5.6 production-reliability / conflict-handling
stem: A synthesis agent receives findings from three subagents: solar investment grew 15% (Bloomberg, January 2024), solar investment grew 22% (IEA, March 2024), and cost-per-watt data. The synthesis agent currently picks the IEA figure because it is more recent. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Always use the most authoritative source (IEA as an international agency) and discard the Bloomberg figure.
options.B: Average the two values (18.5%) and cite both sources to present a balanced view.
options.C: Present both figures with full source attribution and publication dates, annotating that the difference may reflect different reporting periods, methodologies, or scope definitions.
options.D: Flag the conflicting figures and pause report generation until a human researcher resolves the discrepancy.

why_correct: Preserving both data points with provenance — source, date, and potential explanations for the difference — lets the consumer interpret the data correctly. Different publication dates and methodologies explain the discrepancy without requiring the synthesis agent to judge which is 'right'.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Discarding a credible source based on perceived authority silently removes valid data. Both sources are credible, and the difference may reflect different methodologies, scopes, or time periods.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: Averaging conflicting statistics is mathematically misleading. The two figures may measure different scopes (e.g., different regions or investment types), making an average meaningless. The difference needs to be preserved, not merged.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Pausing for human resolution is unnecessary when the difference can be explained by temporal or methodological factors. Proper annotation with provenance resolves the ambiguity without blocking the workflow.

exam_takeaway: Preserving both data points with provenance — source, date, and potential explanations for the difference — lets the consumer interpret the data correctly. Different publication dates and methodologies explain the discrepancy without requiring the synthesis agent to judge which is 'right'.

sources.label: Lesson 5.6: Information Provenance and Multi-Source Synthesis (Conflict handling)
Lesson 5.6: Information Provenance and Multi-Source Synthesis (Temporal awareness)

title: 5.1 context-window-management / facts-block
stem: An agent joins Snowflake revenue data with PostgreSQL customer data via federated queries. To manage context, it progressively summarises earlier results between rounds. After three rounds it reports 'revenue increased in Q3' but cannot give the exact figure ($14.2M), which was lost in summarisation. The user asks for the precise number. What is the most effective fix?

options.A: Re-run the original Snowflake query to retrieve the exact Q3 revenue figure from the source.
options.B: Extract key numerical facts (revenue figures, dates, counts) into a persistent facts block that is included in every prompt, outside the summarised conversation history.
options.C: Increase the context window size so that summarisation is triggered less frequently.
options.D: Instruct the agent to always include exact figures in its summaries rather than qualitative statements.

why_correct: The progressive summarisation trap destroys numerical precision when conversation history is compressed. A persistent facts block preserves exact figures, dates, and identifiers across summarisation rounds, directly solving the data loss problem.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Re-querying works as a recovery tactic but does not prevent the problem from recurring. The agent will summarise again on the next round, losing the figure again. A structural fix is needed.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: A larger context window delays the problem but does not solve it. As queries accumulate, summarisation will eventually compress the figures. The structural fix is to extract key data from the summarisation pipeline entirely.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Prompt-based instructions for summarisation behaviour are unreliable. The model compresses content probabilistically, and instructions cannot guarantee that specific numbers survive multiple rounds of summarisation.

exam_takeaway: The progressive summarisation trap destroys numerical precision when conversation history is compressed. A persistent facts block preserves exact figures, dates, and identifiers across summarisation rounds, directly solving the data loss problem.

Lesson 5.1: Context Window Management (Persistent facts)

title: 5.1 context-window-management / lost-in-the-middle
stem: An agent receives 200 rows of Snowflake financial data and places it mid-prompt, between system instructions and the user's follow-up question. Asked to identify the row with the highest margin, the agent picks the 45th row (margin 32%) over the 142nd row (margin 47%). What cognitive bias is affecting the agent?

options.A: Recency bias — the agent prioritises data appearing near the end of the context window.
options.B: The lost-in-the-middle effect — the agent attends more to data at the beginning and end of the result set, missing the highest-margin row buried in the middle.
options.C: Token limit truncation — the result set exceeds the context window and rows beyond the 100th are silently dropped.
options.D: Anchoring bias — the agent fixates on the first high-margin row it encounters and stops scanning the rest.

why_correct: The lost-in-the-middle effect causes LLMs to attend disproportionately to content at the start and end of long sequences, with reduced attention to material in the middle. Row 142 (the correct answer) sits deep in the middle of the 200-row result set, making it prone to being overlooked.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Recency bias would favour rows near the end of the data, not the 45th row. The 45th row is in the early portion of the result set, which is consistent with the lost-in-the-middle effect, not recency bias.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: If rows were truncated, the agent would not have access to row 142 at all and would report the highest margin from the visible rows. The agent identified a specific wrong row (45th), indicating all data is present but attention is uneven.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Anchoring bias is a human cognitive bias, not a well-documented LLM failure mode for structured data scanning. The observed behaviour — accurate recall at the start and end, poor recall in the middle — is the hallmark of the lost-in-the-middle effect.

exam_takeaway: The lost-in-the-middle effect causes LLMs to attend disproportionately to content at the start and end of long sequences, with reduced attention to material in the middle. Row 142 (the correct answer) sits deep in the middle of the 200-row result set, making it prone to being overlooked.

sources.label: Lesson 5.1: Context Window Management (Lost in the middle)

title: 5.3 long-conversations / silent-suppression
stem: The data platform agent queries three sources in sequence: Snowflake (succeeds), PostgreSQL (returns a connection timeout), and a pricing API (succeeds). The agent silently skips the PostgreSQL failure and produces a report using only Snowflake and API data, without informing the user that customer data is missing. What is the critical design failure?

options.A: The agent should retry the PostgreSQL query automatically with exponential backoff before producing the report.
options.B: The agent silently suppresses the error instead of propagating structured error context that annotates which data sources failed and what coverage the report actually has.
options.C: The agent should abort the entire report if any single data source fails, to avoid producing incomplete results.
options.D: The orchestrator should pre-check all data source connections before allowing the agent to begin querying.

why_correct: Silent error suppression is one of the most dangerous anti-patterns in multi-source systems. The agent must propagate structured error context — identifying which sources failed, what data is missing, and what coverage the final report represents — so the user can make informed decisions about the report's completeness.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Automatic retries are appropriate for transient errors, but the critical failure is that the agent silently suppresses the error. Even after retries exhaust, the agent must surface the failure to the user rather than producing an incomplete report without disclosure.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Aborting on any failure is overly conservative. Partial results with clear coverage annotations are often more useful than no results. The fix is transparency about what is missing, not refusing to produce anything.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Pre-checking connections does not prevent runtime failures (a source can become unavailable between the check and the query). The agent must handle failures gracefully at query time with structured error propagation.

exam_takeaway: Silent error suppression is one of the most dangerous anti-patterns in multi-source systems. The agent must propagate structured error context — identifying which sources failed, what data is missing, and what coverage the final report represents — so the user can make informed decisions about the report's completeness.

title: 5.4 rate-limiting-quotas / compact
stem: A developer has been using the data platform agent in a single extended session for two hours, running complex federated queries, debugging SQL syntax, and iterating on report formatting. The agent now produces noticeably worse SQL and occasionally references table schemas from earlier queries that have since been corrected. What is the most effective intervention?

options.A: Use the /compact command, optionally passing focus instructions, to summarise the conversation so far and free context budget for current-state reasoning.
options.B: Start a completely new session and re-establish all context from scratch.
options.C: Increase the model's temperature parameter to improve creativity and reduce fixation on stale patterns.
options.D: Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to ignore all schema information from more than 30 minutes ago.

why_correct: Extended sessions cause context degradation as stale information (outdated schemas, abandoned approaches) competes with current context. /compact summarises the conversation history into a compressed form, freeing context budget. The optional [instructions] argument lets you bias the summary (for example, 'preserve the corrected schema for the orders table'). It is the documented mitigation for context degradation in long sessions, and the least disruptive option of the four.

per_option_counter_explanations.B: A fresh session discards all accumulated context, including valuable recent work. /compact summarises the existing conversation while preserving the gist of recent work, which is less disruptive than starting over.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Temperature affects output randomness, not context quality. The problem is stale information in the context window polluting the agent's reasoning, not a lack of creative variation.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: The agent has no reliable concept of message timestamps within the context window. Time-based instructions are unenforceable. The structural fix is to compress or remove stale context entries.

exam_takeaway: Extended sessions cause context degradation as stale information (outdated schemas, abandoned approaches) competes with current context. /compact summarises the conversation history into a compressed form, freeing context budget. The optional [instructions] argument lets you bias the summary (for example, 'preserve the corrected schema for the orders table'). It is the documented mitigation for context degradation in long sessions, and the least disruptive option of the four.

title: 5.5 monitoring-observability / aggregate-metrics-trap
stem: The data platform team runs a human review of the agent's federated query reports. Reviewers sample 50 reports and find an overall accuracy rate of 97%. Management approves the system for production. Three weeks later, users report that currency conversion calculations in cross-border revenue reports are wrong 40% of the time. How did the review process fail?

options.A: The sample size of 50 reports was too small to detect a 40% error rate in currency conversions.
options.B: The reviewers used aggregate accuracy metrics that masked category-specific failures. A 97% overall rate hides a 40% error rate on currency conversions if that category is a small fraction of total reports.
options.C: The reviewers were not domain experts in currency conversion and could not identify the errors.
options.D: The agent's accuracy degraded over time due to model drift, and the initial 97% rate was genuinely correct at the time of review.

why_correct: This is the aggregate metrics trap. When a low-frequency report type (cross-border revenue) has high error rates, the overall accuracy metric is dominated by high-frequency, easy report types. Stratified random sampling across report categories would have caught the currency conversion failures.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: A 40% error rate in any category should be detectable in 50 reports — but only if the sample includes enough reports from that category. The problem is sampling strategy, not sample size.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Reviewer expertise is a valid concern but is not the structural failure. Even expert reviewers would miss the problem if the sample did not include enough cross-border reports. The sampling methodology is the root cause.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: LLMs served via API do not experience gradual model drift within a three-week window. The error pattern was present during the review but hidden by aggregate metrics that did not stratify by report category.

exam_takeaway: This is the aggregate metrics trap. When a low-frequency report type (cross-border revenue) has high error rates, the overall accuracy metric is dominated by high-frequency, easy report types. Stratified random sampling across report categories would have caught the currency conversion failures.

sources.label: Lesson 5.5: Human Review and Confidence Calibration (Aggregate metrics trap)

title: 5.6 production-reliability / dual-attribution
stem: The data platform agent produces a report combining Snowflake revenue data and a third-party market sizing API. The Snowflake data shows the company's market share at 12%, whilst the API reports it at 8%. What is the correct provenance approach for the agent's report?

options.A: Use the higher figure (12%) as it comes from the company's own authoritative data source.
options.B: Average the two figures (10%) and report it as the consensus estimate.
options.C: Present both figures with dual attribution — identifying the source, methodology, and time period for each — so the user can evaluate the discrepancy.
options.D: Flag the discrepancy as an error and refuse to include either figure until the data team resolves the conflict.

why_correct: Dual attribution for conflicting data is the correct provenance pattern. The agent must surface both figures with clear claim-source mappings, including the data source, methodology, and temporal context, rather than silently resolving the conflict.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Selecting one figure based on source authority silently discards conflicting information. The user needs both figures with source attribution to make their own judgement.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: Averaging conflicting figures from different methodologies produces a number that neither source supports. This obscures the disagreement rather than surfacing it.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Conflicting sources are not necessarily errors — different methodologies legitimately produce different results. Refusing to report either figure leaves the user with no actionable data when both figures are informative.

exam_takeaway: Dual attribution for conflicting data is the correct provenance pattern. The agent must surface both figures with clear claim-source mappings, including the data source, methodology, and temporal context, rather than silently resolving the conflict.

title: 5.4 rate-limiting-quotas / scratchpad
stem: A data engineer delegates a complex cross-database analysis to the platform agent: join Snowflake billing data with PostgreSQL usage data, apply currency normalisation, and produce a cost-per-user breakdown by region. The agent's context fills rapidly as it accumulates intermediate query results. What is the most effective strategy for managing this multi-step analysis within context limits?

options.A: Write intermediate results to a scratchpad file after each step, then read back only the final aggregated data needed for the cost-per-user calculation.
options.B: Execute all queries in a single SQL statement using cross-database joins to avoid intermediate results entirely.
options.C: Delegate each step to a separate subagent so each runs with a fresh context window, then combine their outputs.
options.D: Summarise intermediate results between steps to reduce their token footprint in the conversation context.

why_correct: Scratchpad files offload intermediate results from the context window. Each step writes its output to a file, keeping the context budget free for the current step's reasoning. The final step reads back only the aggregated data it needs, avoiding the accumulation of raw intermediate results in context.

per_option_counter_explanations.B: Cross-database joins between Snowflake and PostgreSQL are not possible in a single SQL statement — they are separate database systems accessed through different MCP tools. The multi-step approach is architecturally necessary.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Subagent delegation is useful for independent parallel tasks, but this analysis has sequential dependencies (each step depends on the previous step's output). Subagents would need the same intermediate data passed to them, merely shifting the context problem rather than solving it.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Summarising intermediate numerical results risks the progressive summarisation trap — exact billing figures, usage counts, and exchange rates may be compressed into qualitative descriptions, causing calculation errors in subsequent steps.

exam_takeaway: Scratchpad files offload intermediate results from the context window. Each step writes its output to a file, keeping the context budget free for the current step's reasoning. The final step reads back only the aggregated data it needs, avoiding the accumulation of raw intermediate results in context.

title: 5.6 production-reliability / temporal-awareness
stem: The data platform agent generates a quarterly business review report that includes claims such as 'Revenue grew 15% YoY' sourced from Snowflake and 'Market expanded by 22%' sourced from a third-party API. The Snowflake data was last refreshed yesterday, whilst the API data is from a report published six months ago. What provenance metadata must accompany these claims?

options.A: The name of each data source (Snowflake, third-party API) so the user knows where the data came from.
options.B: A confidence score (high/medium/low) for each claim based on the agent's assessment of data quality.
options.C: Claim-source mappings that include the data source, the date or time period the data represents, and the refresh or publication timestamp, enabling the user to assess temporal relevance.
options.D: A footnote at the end of the report listing all data sources used, without linking specific claims to specific sources.

why_correct: Provenance requires claim-source mappings with temporal awareness. Each claim must be linked to its source with date context — the user must see that '15% YoY revenue growth' is from yesterday's Snowflake refresh whilst '22% market expansion' is from a six-month-old third-party report — to assess whether each figure is current enough for the quarterly review.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Source names alone are insufficient. Without temporal context, the user cannot judge whether the data is current enough for a quarterly review. The six-month-old market data may be misleading if presented without its publication date.
per_option_counter_explanations.B: LLM-generated confidence scores are poorly calibrated and do not substitute for factual provenance metadata. The user needs objective source information to make their own quality assessment.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: A generic source list does not create claim-source mappings. The user cannot determine which specific claim came from which source, making it impossible to assess the reliability or currency of individual data points.

exam_takeaway: Provenance requires claim-source mappings with temporal awareness. Each claim must be linked to its source with date context — the user must see that '15% YoY revenue growth' is from yesterday's Snowflake refresh whilst '22% market expansion' is from a six-month-old third-party report — to assess whether each figure is current enough for the quarterly review.

title: 5.1 context-window-management / lost-in-the-middle
stem: Claude Code is synthesising release notes from commit messages, PR descriptions, and changelog entries. During a 200+ commit session, summaries of early commits become vague ('various bug fixes') while recent commits are still detailed accurately. The context window is not full. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The model's temperature is set too high, causing it to generate vague summaries randomly
options.B: The lost-in-the-middle effect causes the model to attend more strongly to information at the beginning and end of context, losing detail for commits in the middle of a long input sequence
options.C: The commit messages for early commits are inherently less detailed than recent ones, so the vague summaries are accurate
options.D: Claude Code applies progressive summarisation to older commits to conserve context for recent ones

why_correct: The lost-in-the-middle effect is a well-documented phenomenon where models attend more strongly to the start and end of long contexts, with reduced attention to middle content. With 200+ commits loaded sequentially, commits in the middle of the sequence receive less attention, producing vague summaries. Processing in smaller batches or reordering critical information to the start and end mitigates this.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Temperature affects output randomness but would produce inconsistent quality across all commits, not a systematic pattern where early commits are vague and recent commits are accurate.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: The question states the vagueness applies to early commits specifically, not commits with poor messages. The systematic pattern (early = vague, recent = detailed) points to a context positioning effect, not source quality variation.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Claude Code does not automatically apply progressive summarisation to tool results within a single processing step. The context window is not full, so there is no space pressure triggering summarisation. The issue is attention distribution across long inputs.

exam_takeaway: The lost-in-the-middle effect is a well-documented phenomenon where models attend more strongly to the start and end of long contexts, with reduced attention to middle content. With 200+ commits loaded sequentially, commits in the middle of the sequence receive less attention, producing vague summaries. Processing in smaller batches or reordering critical information to the start and end mitigates this.

title: 5.1 context-window-management / progressive-summarisation
stem: A docs team processes a 500,000-line codebase by having Claude Code read files and generate docs, instructing it to 'summarise each module after documenting it, then discard the detailed source from context.' After processing 20 modules, the docs for module 21 reference class names from module 3 that were renamed in module 12. What caused this failure?

options.A: Progressive summarisation lost the rename detail: when module 12's summary replaced its source code, the rename was condensed to 'various refactoring changes', so the agent retained module 3's original class names from its earlier summary
options.B: The agent's context window overflowed, causing it to hallucinate class names from earlier modules
options.C: Claude Code cached module 3's source code and served the stale version instead of the updated file on disk
options.D: The model confused similar class names because it processed too many modules in a single session

why_correct: Progressive summarisation is lossy. The summary of module 12 likely compressed the rename into a generic phrase, while module 3's summary still referenced the original class names. When the agent documented module 21, it found conflicting names across summaries and defaulted to the earlier, more prominent reference. Critical cross-module changes like renames must be tracked in a persistent facts block outside summarised context.

per_option_counter_explanations.B: The team explicitly manages context by summarising and discarding source code, so the context window is not overflowing. The problem is the quality of information retained in summaries, not context overflow.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Claude Code does not cache file contents between reads. Each Read tool call fetches the current file from disk. The issue is that summarised context retained old class names, not that file reads returned stale data.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: The question specifies the exact failure: module 21 references class names from module 3 that were renamed in module 12. This is not a confusion issue but a direct consequence of losing the rename detail during progressive summarisation.

exam_takeaway: Progressive summarisation is lossy. The summary of module 12 likely compressed the rename into a generic phrase, while module 3's summary still referenced the original class names. When the agent documented module 21, it found conflicting names across summaries and defaulted to the earlier, more prominent reference. Critical cross-module changes like renames must be tracked in a persistent facts block outside summarised context.

title: 5.3 long-conversations / coverage-annotations
stem: A documentation generation pipeline uses Claude Code to produce docs from three sources: source code comments, existing wiki pages, and API schema files. During a run, the wiki page retrieval fails with a timeout, but the source code and API schema are available. The pipeline currently halts entirely on any source failure. What is the best error handling strategy?

options.A: Retry the wiki retrieval three times with exponential backoff. If all retries fail, halt the pipeline to prevent incomplete documentation
options.B: Return structured error context for the wiki failure (failure type, source URL, partial results if any), proceed with available sources, and mark the generated documentation with explicit gaps noting which sections lack wiki-sourced content
options.C: Silently skip the wiki source and generate documentation from the remaining two sources without noting the omission
options.D: Use the source code comments to infer what the wiki pages would have contained, filling in the gaps with generated content

why_correct: This produces maximum value from available sources while maintaining transparency about what is missing. Structured error context enables intelligent recovery (retry later, alert the team). Explicit gap markers prevent users from trusting incomplete documentation as complete.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Halting the entire pipeline because one of three sources is unavailable wastes the successful results from the other two sources. Documentation from source code and API schemas is still valuable even without wiki content.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Silent omission hides the failure. Users would trust the documentation as complete, not knowing that wiki-sourced context (which may contain critical operational notes or caveats) is missing.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Inferring wiki content from source code produces hallucinated documentation that appears authoritative. Wiki pages often contain operational context, known issues, and tribal knowledge that cannot be inferred from code.

exam_takeaway: This produces maximum value from available sources while maintaining transparency about what is missing. Structured error context enables intelligent recovery (retry later, alert the team). Explicit gap markers prevent users from trusting incomplete documentation as complete.

title: 5.4 rate-limiting-quotas / context-degradation
stem: A documentation team working across a 500,000-line codebase notices that Claude Code's responses become less specific after extensive file exploration. What is the term for this degradation and what is the primary mitigation in Claude Code?

options.A: Token exhaustion — mitigated by increasing the model's max_tokens parameter
options.B: Context degradation — mitigated by using scratchpad files to persist key findings outside the conversation context, and delegating exploration to subagents to isolate verbose output
options.C: Hallucination drift — mitigated by lowering the temperature to zero for deterministic output
options.D: Prompt injection — mitigated by sanitising file contents before they enter the context window

why_correct: Context degradation occurs when the model loses grip on specific details as verbose tool output accumulates in the conversation. Scratchpad files persist findings on disk where they can be re-read as needed. Subagent delegation isolates verbose exploration output from the main agent's context budget.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: max_tokens controls response length, not the model's ability to retain and reference earlier context. The degradation occurs because verbose exploration output fills the context window, not because responses are truncated.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: The issue is not hallucination from randomness but loss of specificity from context overload. Temperature zero produces deterministic output but does not help the model retain specific findings from earlier in a long context.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Prompt injection is a security concern involving malicious content in inputs. The described problem — responses becoming vague after extensive exploration — is context degradation from accumulated verbose output, not a security issue.

exam_takeaway: Context degradation occurs when the model loses grip on specific details as verbose tool output accumulates in the conversation. Scratchpad files persist findings on disk where they can be re-read as needed. Subagent delegation isolates verbose exploration output from the main agent's context budget.

title: 5.5 monitoring-observability / reviewer-capacity
stem: Claude Code generates API reference pages for 150 endpoints across three categories: payment processing (30 endpoints, high regulatory risk), internal tooling (80 endpoints, low risk), and public data queries (40 endpoints, moderate risk). The team cannot manually review all 150. How should they structure human review?

options.A: Randomly sample 15% of all endpoints (approximately 23 pages) for review, ensuring a representative cross-section
options.B: Use stratified sampling: review 100% of payment processing docs (30 pages), 10% of public data query docs (4 pages), and 5% of internal tooling docs (4 pages), totalling 38 pages with effort concentrated on highest-risk content
options.C: Review only the payment processing endpoints since they are the highest risk, and trust Claude Code's output for the remaining 120 endpoints
options.D: Have Claude Code self-assess each generated page with a confidence score and only review pages where confidence falls below 80%

why_correct: Stratified sampling allocates review effort proportional to risk. Payment processing documentation has regulatory implications warranting full review. Public data queries affect external users and deserve moderate scrutiny. Internal tooling has the lowest blast radius and can tolerate the lightest review. This achieves thorough coverage of critical content within a manageable review budget.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Uniform random sampling treats all endpoints equally, but payment processing endpoints carry much higher risk. A 15% sample might only include 4-5 payment endpoints, inadequately covering the highest-risk category.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Completely skipping review for 120 endpoints risks undetected errors in public-facing documentation. Even low-risk internal tooling docs should have some sample review to catch systematic generation issues that might affect all categories.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: LLM self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated. Claude Code may report high confidence on pages with subtle factual errors (e.g., incorrect parameter types, wrong default values) because the generated text is fluent and internally consistent.

exam_takeaway: Stratified sampling allocates review effort proportional to risk. Payment processing documentation has regulatory implications warranting full review. Public data queries affect external users and deserve moderate scrutiny. Internal tooling has the lowest blast radius and can tolerate the lightest review. This achieves thorough coverage of critical content within a manageable review budget.

title: 5.6 production-reliability / structured-provenance
stem: A docs team has Claude Code generate architecture guides by synthesising source code, inline comments, commit messages, and ADRs. After several edits, the guides no longer indicate which statements came from which source. A developer later questions whether a specific architectural constraint in a guide is still valid. What approach preserves source attribution?

options.A: Instruct Claude Code to add footnotes to the generated documentation citing the original source for each statement
options.B: Maintain structured provenance metadata alongside each documentation section, mapping claims to their source files, line numbers, and retrieval dates, stored as machine-readable data separate from the prose content
options.C: Keep all original source files unchanged in a reference directory so developers can manually trace any claim back to its origin
options.D: Version-control the documentation and use git blame to trace each line back to the commit that created it

why_correct: Structured provenance metadata survives editing because it is stored as data fields (e.g., JSON or YAML frontmatter) separate from the prose. When a developer questions a claim, they can trace it to the exact source file and line number. The retrieval date indicates whether the source was current when the documentation was generated.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Prose footnotes are fragile — they are lost or degraded during subsequent editing passes, summarisation, or reformatting. The team has already experienced this problem through 'several iterations of editing.'
per_option_counter_explanations.C: Preserving source files without explicit mappings forces developers to manually search through potentially hundreds of files to verify a single claim. This is not scalable and does not indicate which specific source informed which specific documentation statement.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: git blame traces authorship of documentation lines to commits, not to the source material that informed those lines. A commit message might say 'update architecture guide' without indicating that a specific statement came from ADR-047 or a comment in auth-service/src/middleware.ts.

exam_takeaway: Structured provenance metadata survives editing because it is stored as data fields (e.g., JSON or YAML frontmatter) separate from the prose. When a developer questions a claim, they can trace it to the exact source file and line number. The retrieval date indicates whether the source was current when the documentation was generated.

title: 5.4 rate-limiting-quotas / scratchpad
stem: A docs team asks Claude Code to audit documentation coverage across a 500,000-line codebase. After reading 30 files via the Read tool, the conversation is approaching the context limit and earlier tool results will be summarised away by auto-compaction. The agent still needs that earlier information to complete the audit. What is the best strategy?

options.A: Increase the context window size so that all 30+ file contents can be held simultaneously without trimming
options.B: Have the agent write structured findings (file name, public API list, documentation status) to a scratchpad file after processing each source file, then reference the scratchpad for the final audit report instead of relying on in-context tool results
options.C: Process all files in a single Read tool call by passing a glob pattern, so the results arrive in one untrimmed block
options.D: Run /compact after every 10 files to free up context space for the next batch of file reads

why_correct: A scratchpad file persists on disk and can be re-read at any time, unlike in-context tool results that are trimmed as new results arrive. By extracting and recording the essential findings (not the full file contents) after each file read, the agent decouples its knowledge from context window limits. The final audit reads the compact scratchpad rather than needing all source files in context.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: The context window has a fixed maximum size. A 500,000-line codebase cannot fit entirely in context regardless of configuration. Tool result trimming exists specifically because holding all file contents simultaneously is not feasible.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: The Read tool reads individual files, not glob patterns. Even if multiple files could be read at once, a single massive result block would itself be trimmed or would consume the entire context budget, preventing the agent from reasoning about the results.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: /compact summarises the conversation, which may discard the specific findings from earlier file reads. The problem is preserving information, not just freeing space. Compacting without first persisting findings to disk loses the very data the audit needs.

exam_takeaway: A scratchpad file persists on disk and can be re-read at any time, unlike in-context tool results that are trimmed as new results arrive. By extracting and recording the essential findings (not the full file contents) after each file read, the agent decouples its knowledge from context window limits. The final audit reads the compact scratchpad rather than needing all source files in context.

title: 5.5 monitoring-observability / human-review-criticality
stem: A documentation team uses Claude Code to generate runbooks for incident response procedures. The generated runbooks include specific command sequences and escalation paths. Why is human review especially critical for this type of generated documentation?

options.A: Because Claude Code cannot execute bash commands, so it cannot verify the commands it documents
options.B: Because runbooks are executed under pressure during incidents, where an incorrect command sequence or escalation path could worsen an outage, and LLM-generated content may be fluent but factually incorrect in ways that are hard to detect without domain expertise
options.C: Because Claude Code does not have access to production systems and therefore generates runbooks based on outdated development environment configurations
options.D: Because runbooks require formatting that Claude Code cannot produce, such as flowcharts and decision trees

why_correct: Runbooks have an unusually high blast radius: they are followed during stressful incidents when operators may not critically evaluate each step. An incorrect command (e.g., wrong database connection string, incorrect rollback procedure) could escalate an incident. LLM-generated instructions appear authoritative and well-structured, making subtle errors harder to spot without expert review.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Claude Code can execute bash commands via the Bash tool. However, the ability to run commands does not mean the generated runbook procedures are safe, complete, or appropriate for production incident response.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: The question is about why human review is critical, not about Claude Code's system access. Even if Claude Code had production access, human review would still be essential because generated procedures could be logically incorrect or operationally dangerous.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Claude Code can produce Markdown-based documentation including structured decision trees. The formatting capability is not the reason human review is critical — the risk of factually incorrect procedures under incident pressure is.

exam_takeaway: Runbooks have an unusually high blast radius: they are followed during stressful incidents when operators may not critically evaluate each step. An incorrect command (e.g., wrong database connection string, incorrect rollback procedure) could escalate an incident. LLM-generated instructions appear authoritative and well-structured, making subtle errors harder to spot without expert review.

title: 5.6 production-reliability / structured-provenance
stem: A docs team has Claude Code synthesise an API reference guide from source across 50 modules. The guide states 'the authentication service supports OAuth2, SAML, and API key authentication' with no indication of which source files informed this. Six months later, after a major refactor, the team needs to verify whether the statement is still accurate. What is the core provenance failure and how should it be prevented?

options.A: The failure is that the guide was not version-controlled. Storing it in git would allow the team to trace the statement back to the commit that generated it
options.B: The failure is loss of claim-to-source traceability during synthesis. Each factual claim should carry structured provenance linking it to specific source files (e.g., auth-service/src/providers/*.ts) and retrieval timestamps, enabling targeted re-verification of affected claims after refactoring
options.C: The failure is that Claude Code hallucinated the authentication methods. The team should run a separate verification pass to confirm each claim against the source code
options.D: The failure is that the documentation was generated in a single pass. Processing modules incrementally with human review after each module would catch inaccuracies before synthesis

why_correct: Without claim-to-source mappings, the team must re-audit the entire codebase to verify a single statement. Structured provenance (source file, line range, retrieval date) makes verification targeted: check whether auth-service/src/providers/ still contains OAuth2, SAML, and API key implementations. The retrieval timestamp signals when the claim was last verified.

per_option_counter_explanations.A: Version control tracks when documentation was written, not which source code files informed a specific claim. Knowing that the statement was generated on a certain date does not help the team identify which files to re-check after refactoring.
per_option_counter_explanations.C: The question does not indicate the claim was hallucinated — it may have been accurate when generated. The problem is that six months later, the team has no way to efficiently verify or update the claim because they cannot trace it back to specific source files.
per_option_counter_explanations.D: Incremental review improves generation-time accuracy but does not solve the six-months-later verification problem. Without provenance metadata linking claims to sources, the team still cannot efficiently determine which files to re-check after refactoring.

exam_takeaway: Without claim-to-source mappings, the team must re-audit the entire codebase to verify a single statement. Structured provenance (source file, line range, retrieval date) makes verification targeted: check whether auth-service/src/providers/ still contains OAuth2, SAML, and API key implementations. The retrieval timestamp signals when the claim was last verified.
